Current code representations are limited to linear formats such as tokens or abstract syntax trees, but these fall short in extracting essential structural information. We introduce a graph-based code representation that captures key properties and their interconnections, effectively modeling code for tasks like semantic analysis and manipulation. By converting various code snippets into graphs, we can identify entities like classes, interfaces, and functions and their relationships, enabling code understanding and manipulation with graph-based techniques. We apply node classification in the graph representation to identify code components and achieve state-of-the-art results on a semantic code duplication task, outperforming previous methods. Additionally, we show that our method can be adapted for code summarization and improvement tasks. The code and representation are available on GitHub at https://github.com/krishan-goyal/code-graph.

This paper presents a computational method for simultaneous variable selection and network reconstruction using Graphical Lasso. The proposed scheme incorporates a penalized estimation technique and a constrained optimization method, derived from Second-Order Cone Programming, to tackle the Graphical Lasso problem. The mathematical properties and convergence of this computational method are analyzed and its superiority over other approaches is demonstrated through high-order asymptotic analysis. Furthermore, the method's efficiency in practice is verified through numerical experiments and its application to real-world data is showcased in two case studies. The method is implemented in the R package GLSOCP.

We present a model based on the $A_4$ group that explains why neutrinos have masses so small, while allowing for normal ordering of neutrino masses. In this model, the phases of neutrino oscillations arise from a combination of the symmetry breaking and the periodic rotation of the flavon field, which itself is caused by a radion mediated by a heavy scalar. This results in a discrete, family dependent, continuous chiral rotation, leading to a small neutrino mass. We also demonstrate that this type of mechanism can generate masses for charged fermions, with the exception of a single charged fermion whose mass is determined by a type I seesaw mechanism. This includes a discussion of the constraints imposed by lepton universality, the mass of the Z boson, and the stability of the proton. We find that this model is consistent with all experimental data, including recent results from the LHC. Furthermore, we examine the potential for direct detection of the scalar responsible for neutrino masses in future high-energy colliders. Finally, we discuss the possibility of testing this model at low energy in neutrinoless double beta decay experiments. Due to the significant mass splitting between the lightest and second lightest scalar states, we find that this model may be testable at low energy in the coming decade. Neural architecture search has seen significant progress in recent years, but most current approaches are limited to searching within defined spaces of architectures. We introduce a novel framework that empowers comprehensive architecture search within vast, abstract search spaces that are not initially defined. Our method, called Meta Architecture Search, enables the discovery of novel architectures from these abstract spaces. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully searching for new architectures in the areas of image recognition and graph-based neural networks, and our results show that our method outperforms alternative approaches. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexeyguz/MetaArchitectureSearch.

The findings demonstrate that a binary threshold policy is both optimal and guaranteed to exist. Federated Learning's efficiency can be enhanced by Federated Distillation, a data-sharing approach, especially when compared to Federated Learning methods. We've developed a new Federated Distillation protocol that significantly reduces communication load and computational costs. By testing this protocol on image classification tasks, the results show it achieves comparable accuracy to model-based Federated Learning, while also outperforming existing distillation-based Federated Learning methods. Moreover, Federated Distillation has the advantage of producing more interpretable and diverse student models. The source code for the new protocol is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexeygogolev/fed_distillation.

Named Data Networking (NDN) is a data-centric networking paradigm that allows direct access to requested data, enabling faster and more efficient application deployment in distributed computing networks. To support next-generation service applications, particularly high-throughput ones, in such networks, we introduce a new data management strategy called Hierarchical Caching with Aggressive Forwarding (HCAF). This approach optimizes cache placement and data transmission by strategically repositioning data fragments in the network, leading to a substantial increase in overall network throughput. Our comprehensive simulation results demonstrate the substantial efficacy of HCAF. Notably, HCAF outperforms the current best caching methods by 11% to 20%, depending on the scenario. This approach can be applied to various NDN-based service deployments to significantly boost their performance. Our open-source implementation of HCAF is available at https://github.com/ndnHCAF/hcaf. We create an optical illusion of a 2D electronic lattice, specifically herringbone or chessboard-shaped, which exhibits Dirac cones at its 'corners'. This specific structure, known as a Weyl semimetal in the electronic realm, has been replicated as an optical illusion in two dimensions. When viewed from a distance or in a large-scale perspective, the illusion breaks down due to the Moiré effect caused by the close proximity of the 'atoms', but this can be resolved by increasing the size or scale of the structure. Several versions of this optical illusion are presented, showcasing its potential applications in visual arts. Moreover, we explore the possibility of using this illusion to educate people about the characteristics of Dirac cones and the principles of quantum physics. By manipulating the 'atoms' in the lattice, we can alter its appearance, effectively demonstrating the Hückel model's description of atomic interactions and electron bonding. This provides a unique, visually engaging tool for explaining complex 2D bonding structures to a non-technical audience. Several variations of this optical illusion are also presented, highlighting its artistic and educational value. As a supplementary resource, a step-by-step guide is included to aid in creating these 3D illusions on a flat surface. We have developed a novel algorithm for non-stationary risk-sensitive reinforcement learning that accurately estimates a policy's long-term expected reward within a predetermined error margin. The proposed method employs a variation budget, which is a maximum allowed change in the Markov decision process's dynamics. Under the assumption that this variation budget is known, our algorithm provides a confidence interval for the estimated reward. This research is the first to offer such an estimate in a non-stationary risk-sensitive setting, building on previous work that required significantly tighter constraints. The algorithm's performance was verified through both theoretical analysis and experimental testing. The code is publicly available on the repository https://github.com/zheng-chen-1/RiskSensitive-RL.git.

This controller aggregates the information and sends optimized updates back to the nodes. We also demonstrate the practical utility of our findings by improving the performance of existing distributed training platforms. Specifically, we use the Apache MXNet system and show that our approach leads to significant gains in convergence speed. Our code is available online.

Cross-domain recommendation aims to enhance recommendation accuracy by leveraging information from multiple target domains. However, current approaches often overlook the diverse characteristics of target domains, treating them as if they have similar preferences. In reality, each domain has its own unique user interests, making it unrealistic to assume they share preferences. To address this issue, we propose the Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) model, which capitalizes on user sparsity across multiple domains to provide personalized recommendations. By doing so, MSDCR outperforms state-of-the-art cross-domain recommendation methods, demonstrating the value of domain diversity in enhancing recommendation accuracy. Furthermore, our model's ability to automatically identify domain characteristics without manual labeling enables data analysts to gain actionable insights. To validate our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on three real-world datasets, showcasing its superiority over existing cross-domain recommendation techniques. This research investigates how binarizing weights and activations in deep neural networks affects their ability to generalize. We initially found that this process often hinders generalization, but this led us to a more significant discovery: even state-of-the-art activation quantization can cause neural networks to learn poorly generalized singular vectors. These suboptimal vectors are then effectively filtered out when the network is fully trained. Building on this insight, we developed a novel training method that separates and eliminates undesirable vectors, resulting in improved generalization performance. Experiments demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing schemes and yields comparable results to non-quantized baselines. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/chenzhengyue/vecfilter.

Quantum systems' fundamental properties are encapsulated in their entropy principle. In free fermionic systems, this entropy is calculated using the von Neumann density matrix, while in interacting systems it can be computed using a generalized free fermionic theory. By applying this approach to a one-dimensional system, we derive the bulk entropy of the associated higher-dimensional bulk space. Our findings reveal that the bulk entropy adheres to the principles of the Holographic Entropy Cone and AdS/BCS correspondence, implying that the boundary entropy is solely determined by its smallest non-negative eigenvalue. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the boundary entropy exhibits a sudden death phenomenon, analogous to the one observed in quantum information decay. Our results provide a theoretical framework for the entropy principle of quantum systems and offer a new approach to studying the bulk entropy of higher-dimensional bulk spaces associated with one-dimensional boundary systems. This method may also be applicable to more complex systems, potentially enabling the development of new entropy estimation techniques. Our findings are also relevant to the study of superconductors and other quantum systems, as well as the AdS/BCS correspondence and the black hole information paradox. Our work opens up new avenues for the study of bulk entropy and its connection to boundary entropy in quantum systems. A recent breakthrough in classical verification of quantum computation has led to a direct, single-server protocol with a time complexity of O(poly-k log(k)) and a smaller communication overhead of O(log(k)/poly(k)) bandwidth. In this context, 'k' denotes the number of qubits, and 'poly(k)' represents a polynomial function of 'k'. We enhance this protocol by developing a more efficient single-server approach with a time complexity of O(poly-k log(k)^{1.5}) and a lower communication overhead of O(log(k)/poly(k)) bandwidth. Furthermore, we introduce a two-server protocol with a time complexity of O(poly-k log(k)^{0.75}) and a communication overhead of O(poly-k log(k)^{0.25}) bandwidth. Both of these new protocols leverage a modified version of the Helsing-Hästö algorithm for efficient evaluation of polynomial systems. In doing so, we resolve a computational problem that had previously hindered the development of efficient classical verification of quantum computation. This research introduces a novel approach to analyzing interconnected time series 
by leveraging the properties of cross-recurrence plots in a dimensionless framework. 
Specifically, the proposed method extends cross-recurrence plot analysis to multi-segmented 
time series and weights each recurrence by the persistence of cross-recurrences. 
Applied to the FTSE 100 stock exchange index, this approach successfully identifies 
significant patterns and events, including the 2008 global financial crisis and two distinct 
periods of high market volatility characterized by varying dynamics. 
Furthermore, the method's time-dependent nature allows for the detection of critical instances 
and the quantification of cross-recurrence plot patterns' temporal significance. 
Compared to other methods, the persistence-weighted cross-recurrence plot analysis outperforms 
in terms of sensitivity and accuracy, while also offering a more detailed understanding of the 
recurrent patterns and connections between time series. 
Ultimately, this approach provides a valuable tool for the in-depth analysis and interpretation 
of complex financial time series data.

Predicting click-through rates accurately for a wide range of advertisements across various platforms is a crucial task in advertising systems. However, current models often struggle with new ads that have limited historical data, resulting in significant prediction errors. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach that leverages the collective knowledge gained from high-quality existing ads to enhance prediction performance for new ads. The approach involves representing new ads in a search space based on their semantic similarities to existing ads with high predicted click-through rates. By doing so, new ads benefit from the learned patterns in the top-performing ads, resulting in improved prediction performance. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, with up to 34% improved absolute prediction error compared to the baseline methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenXinyu2019/CrossAD.

Label availability is a significant constraint for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), limiting their practical applications. To overcome this issue, we present a pseudo-labeling framework that generates high-quality pseudo-labels for unmarked graph nodes. The framework consists of two interconnected components: a node representation enhancer that improves pseudo-label accuracy by selecting nodes with confident labels, and a label corrector that refines pseudo-labels by identifying label errors. The enhancer and corrector components are based on complementary principles and utilize local node features and neighboring structures. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that the enhancer can be viewed as a maximum entropy estimator and the corrector can be seen as a maximum correlation seeker. Experimental results show that our pseudo-labeling framework achieves superior performance compared to existing methods on multiple benchmark datasets. Additionally, the research provides a revised value of 1.87(4) eb for $^{71}$Ge. These findings not only set a new standard for measurement accuracy but also offer valuable data for the development of theoretical models describing the structure of exotic nuclei. Researchers introduced a novel technique, ISOLmergingTRAP, for accurately measuring the mass of short-lived, unusual nuclei. This technique combines isotope separation with a precise trapping method to determine mass. Initially, the technique was demonstrated using the RIKEN Radioisotope Beam Factory's ISOL system and the TRAP at RIKEN, focusing on the nucleus $^{69}\mathrm{Cu}$. The ISOLmergingTRAP technique yielded a mass measurement with an exceptionally low margin of error of 120 keV or less. This technique is now prepared for high-precision mass measurements of a wide variety of short-lived, unusual nuclei. Furthermore, the technique has significant potential for detecting exotic nuclear phenomena, such as nuclear shell effects and abnormal nuclear deformations. Lastly, the technique can be optimized to measure masses with an even lower margin of error, making it a valuable tool for nuclear physics research. 2023 The Authors. This study explores the behavior of interacting agents who form opinions under limited confidence. Each agent only considers the opinions of their immediate social circle, leading to a division in the social network. As a result, the agents' opinions split into two distinct and separate clusters, characterized by the agents within each cluster holding similar opinions. This phenomenon was discovered through the analysis of a complex social network, resulting in a theoretical understanding of its cause and effect. Experiments conducted on various social network architectures have confirmed these findings. Additionally, the research shows that the quality of the division is directly influenced by the level of confidence constraint. Under extreme constraints, the social network may become fragmented into multiple clusters. A key aspect of this research is that it demonstrates the formation of these clusters without any underlying order in the agents' opinions. Furthermore, the findings reveal a connection between the social network's architecture and the agents' opinions, leading to a deeper understanding of a complex and dynamic system. Automatically generating code from natural language specifications is a complex task. This paper explores the reverse process: creating specifications to produce code. A system is presented that generates program specifications based on flow charts drawn by users, allowing the system to synthesize code from these specifications. Evaluations were conducted in a controlled setting, achieving an accuracy rate of 70.59% in synthesizing working code. Additionally, the system was able to translate specifications drawn by users into working programs, reaching an accuracy rate of 73.08%. Both of these results outperform a baseline text-based approach. A user study revealed a positive response to the system, with users indicating a 75% likelihood of using it in real-world scenarios. The system's specifications were also found to be clear and easy to understand, with users able to write working programs 91.67% of the time based solely on these specifications. A comparative study showed that the system excelled at synthesizing code from specifications compared to other approaches, particularly in scenarios involving nested loops. The system's specifications were also found to be more readable than text-based specifications in a subjective evaluation. A detailed analysis of incorrect synthesizations revealed common challenges faced by the system. These findings contribute to the understanding of the relationship between visual and textual representations of program specifications. We introduce locality masked RNNs, a type of recurrent neural network with a sparse transition matrix, allowing for substantial memory reduction during training. Our research shows that locality masked RNNs are both efficient in terms of memory usage and data requirements, outperforming fully-connected RNNs. Additionally, we found that transition matrix sparsity is a key factor that determines the performance of locality masked RNNs. Based on these findings, we developed a transition matrix initialization method that balances high accuracy and efficient resource utilization. Our results indicate that locality masked RNNs can achieve comparable accuracy to fully-connected RNNs, while also reducing memory needs and data requirements by a factor of four. Our implementation is now available.

Three-dimensional local image features are commonly used for various applications in computer vision. The concept of symmetry in local features is typically limited to planar symmetry. This paper introduces a novel way to describe symmetry in local features within three-dimensional spaces. We define a specific type of symmetry, denoted as SP-symmetry, which can be applied to any vector representation of local features. By utilizing the concept of group theory, we establish that each SP-invariant feature possesses certain characteristics. These characteristics enable the creation of symmetry orbits, which serve as a basis for our research. We also devise a method to generate characteristic functions for these orbits and propose a way to calculate weights for local feature coding. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experiments conducted on multiple datasets. The associated code can be found on the repository https://github.com/zhengyue1205/SP-symmetry.

Previous research has not provided a clear explanation for this variability, and its mechanisms of action are not well understood. This study employs the dynamic collective mechanism, a theoretical framework for analyzing neural network behavior, to investigate the purpose of GAP in residual networks. The findings suggest that GAP serves to collectively represent model features at different scales, and the variable performance of GAP depends on the quality of these features. Moreover, the number of GAP units should be proportional to the depth of the model for optimal results. The study also presents a simple yet effective method for improving the representation of features at different scales, resulting in improved classification accuracy on various datasets. Deep neural networks require substantial training to achieve high segmentation accuracy, but this process becomes even more challenging when working with limited labeled data. To address this limitation, a novel approach called Depth-Net is introduced, which leverages depth estimation from unlabeled videos for unsupervised pre-training of segmentation networks. Specifically, Depth-Net combines two components: a feature extractor and a depth estimation model, to predict scene depths without relying on labeled data. The pre-trained model is then fine-tuned using labeled images, and it is demonstrated that integrating a segmentation head can effectively predict scene depths with high accuracy even after being transferred to new domains. Notably, the proposed method achieves competitive results on KITTI and SceneFlow datasets without requiring any labeled data, and it outperforms several baseline approaches on the SemanticKITTI dataset. Furthermore, Depth-Net is shown to enhance the performance of several segmentation models on the SemanticKITTI dataset, and it is successfully applied to a real-world autonomous driving dataset. Building upon the success of Chinese word segmentation via subword models, we explore adapting this approach to Japanese, however, we find existing models are not directly applicable due to significant differences in language characteristics. To overcome this, we develop a custom Japanese word segmentation model incorporating subword units, pre-trained word embeddings, and a graph-based alignment mechanism to handle polysemous characters and multiple morphemes. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed model over baseline models. Moreover, we provide an open-source implementation of this model.

This study examines the sharing of links on Stack Overflow to understand how users engage with off-site resources while problem-solving. We analyzed over 1.5 million link-sharing instances and found that most occur within short time intervals, indicating they are often part of users' question-forming processes. While a significant proportion of links shared involve external resources, our findings suggest that users primarily utilize Stack Overflow's own references. This discovery implies potential improvements for the platform include integrating third-party resources and enhancing user experience through features like search suggestions and related questions. Building on these insights, we propose several design interventions to help users better find relevant information on Stack Overflow. Our analysis provides a foundation for further research into users' behavior when sharing links on the platform. We've developed a new method to analyze how Self-Interacting Dark Matter models behave in galaxy clusters by comparing them to Cold Dark Matter models. This involves matching the distribution of dark matter in galaxy clusters observed by X-ray satellites. Our method can determine the cross-section of Dark Matter particles and how its density responds to baryonic feedback processes that affect galaxy clusters. Applying this method to data from the Bullet Cluster, we've found that SIDM models with high mass cannot fit the data, but models with mass similar to the mass of WIMPs are still possible. Our results also suggest that SIDM models are more sensitive to baryonic feedback processes than CDM models. To confirm our findings, we've simulated galaxy clusters under different SIDM and CDM models and observed that the distribution of dark matter in galaxy clusters is more affected by baryonic feedback processes in SIDM models. Our results show that future observations of galaxy clusters by X-ray satellites could rule out or confirm SIDM models with mass similar to the mass of WIMPs. Our code and simulations are available for public use.

The results also indicated that a one-way information flow is generally ineffective. The findings provide insights for developing online climate change communication strategies. The methodology used can be adapted for other areas of communication. The code and a tutorial on this method are available online for reproduction and further research.

Deep learning models, specifically Artificial Neural Networks, have seen significant advancements in various fields, but their computational power comes with substantial energy costs. In contrast, biological neurons operate efficiently due to their temporary, event-driven signals, which motivates the development of Spiking Neural Networks emulating this behavior. We introduce a novel, compact method for generating SNNs from conventional CNNs, which reduces energy consumption and increases model portability. Our approach enables the creation of fully spiking models, which can be trained end-to-end using backpropagation. We test its effectiveness on various image classification tasks and observe a substantial decrease in energy consumption and computational costs, along with improved memory usage and performance. Notably, our models exhibit high accuracy on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets while using significantly fewer parameters and energy. This method has potential applications in developing event-driven, power-efficient hardware for artificial intelligence. The source code is publicly available on GitHub. https://github.com/krishanmukul/CompactSNN.

A computational method for solving nonlinear eigenvalue problems is proposed, utilizing the minimal rational interpolation method to approximate eigenvalues and eigenvectors. The MRIM employs polynomial interpolation with a rational function, which is often used for eigenvalue problems involving complex constraints. The method is modified to solve nonlinear eigenproblems of the form $A\mathbf{x} = \mu B\mathbf{x}$, where $A$ and $B$ are Hermitian matrices. The MRIM is applied in two forms: with exact rational interpolation and with approximate Newton iterations. The approximate Newton variant is found to be more efficient, especially for larger problem sizes. The approach is compared to other state-of-the-art methods for nonlinear eigenproblems and shown to be a faster alternative. The methodology is tested on a variety of eigenvalue problems, involving matrix functions such as $e^{\sqrt{A}}$ and $\ln(B^{-1/2}A B^{1/2})$, as well as a problem from quantum mechanics. The results indicate that the MRIM is a suitable tool for solving a range of nonlinear eigenvalue problems. Creating testable design specifications for embedded software is crucial, 
yet developing and implementing these specifications is often challenging 
due to interactions with external peripherals that require specific timing.
To address this issue, we developed TDDatapath, an approach that facilitates 
the creation and testing of design specifications within embedded systems.
TDDatapath optimizes hardware-software cooperation to automate testing 
by allowing software bugs to propagate as bit patterns onto hardware buses.
This results in detectable errors that can be pinpointed using existing hardware 
debuggers, thus eliminating the need for custom debugging hardware.
Our approach was successfully tested on a Zynq FPGA platform and demonstrated 
an average error detection rate of 85% in simulating software bugs for various 
benchmark applications. Additionally, we provide a publicly accessible GitHub 
repository containing detailed implementation guidelines and a set of testable design 
specifications for datapath components. Our methodology can be found in the video 
recordings and project documentation included in this repository.

The distribution of stars in the center of the galaxy NGC 1042 shows a distinct break in its density profile, indicating a possible break point in the density distribution. By analyzing data from the Hubble Space Telescope, we observed a break in the density profile at a distance of approximately 0.8 arcseconds from the galaxy's center, which can be attributed to the influence of a supermassive black hole with a mass of 3.4 million solar masses. This break point is likely a photoionization front formed by the intense radiation emitted by hot stars within the galaxy's central bulge. Furthermore, we discovered a possible dust ring around the galaxy's central bulge, which could be obscured by a patch of dust with a diameter of 0.5 arcseconds. We've developed a general framework for the mathematical scrutiny of ecosystems composed of multiple species that interact with each other in complex ways, influenced by random events and immigration. Our approach allows for a detailed analysis of these ecosystems' long-term behaviors, even when their dynamics are non-recurring and chaotic. We've demonstrated this methodology by solving a specific problem involving the competition of two species for limited resources, with one species capable of protecting itself through a defensive mechanism that comes at a cost. Our findings show that species with defensive capabilities have a significant advantage, but only up to a certain point, beyond which the vulnerable species thrives due to the cost of defense. This counterintuitive result is confirmed by experiments in a laboratory setting, involving the interaction of two bacterial species competing for nutrients in a microbial ecosystem. Our study provides a valuable tool for understanding the intricate balance of ecosystems, even when their behaviors seem unpredictable in the long term. Our work is also relevant to a broader range of applications, including bio-chemical networks and financial systems. The trap's potential, calculated using finite element analysis, localizes cold atoms captured in a laser beam. The integrated circuit has been successfully tested in a magneto-optical trap that utilizes a 1060 nm laser, yielding a population count of 10^4 atoms within its 1.5 mm x 1.5 mm surface area. The development of this micro-trap holds promise for the integration of optical atomic clocks and sensing systems onto a single chip. The process of mass accretion onto a black hole is influenced by various factors, 
including the angular momentum of an infalling gas cloud. This paper examines 
how angular momentum impacts accretion rates in the vicinity of a black hole. 
A new analytical framework is developed to model accretion patterns. This model 
relies on a boundary condition that reflects the angular momentum within the 
cloud, leading to a modified Shakura-Sunyaev solution. By applying this model, 
it's shown that a cloud's angular momentum can result in a reduction of mass 
accretion rates compared to non-rotating systems. Furthermore, the model's results 
are compared to numerical simulations, demonstrating good agreement in all 
examined cases. The developed framework can be employed to study accretion processes 
in the presence of cloud rotation. Additionally, the model's results have been 
made available in the form of an online calculator.

In vehicular communications, high-speed and high-mobility scenarios make it difficult for channel estimation to function accurately. To overcome this challenge, a pilot allocation strategy is proposed that dynamically adjusts the quantity of training symbols based on the channel's expected variability. The proposed approach utilizes an adaptive Gaussian mixture model to identify and track channels, and estimates the number of hidden lanes and vehicles through a Beroulk-Zhaki bound-based method. The results show that the proposed pilot allocation method outperforms random allocation, especially in situations with limited high-speed vehicle mobility data. Furthermore, the approach demonstrates its capability to recover lane structure information and simultaneously track channels with high precision. The associated source code can be accessed at https://github.com/NeuralV2X/Adaptive-Pilots-V2X.

This study introduces a novel approach to automatic colorization of grayscale images using a combination of techniques inspired by Quake, a popular neural network for image restoration. The method addresses two primary challenges in colorization: generating visually plausible colors and preserving image details. The first challenge is overcome by employing a 3D convolutional network that produces color information. The second challenge is addressed through the use of a Quake-based regression network, which refines the generated colors based on the original image. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated on two datasets, including a custom dataset of medical images. The results show that the method outperforms existing colorization techniques, particularly in preserving image edges. We present a numerical method for estimating the weights of highly expressive Artificial Neural Networks, which relies on the Frechet Differentiability of Layer-Normalization and the implicit function theorem. This approach involves an under-determined system of equations, which we resolve using a regularized version of the fixed point iteration. The resulting weights are then filtered to remove unnecessary, redundant connections. Our method is validated through experiments involving the most complex networks architecture, achieving comparable results to state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, our approach outperforms existing methods in scenarios with limited data availability. The task of relation extraction aims to identify specific connections between entities mentioned in a text. Current methods excel at extracting well-known relationships but struggle with less common ones. To address this limitation, we propose a data augmentation technique that improves the diversity of existing datasets, allowing models to better recognize a broader range of relationships. This technique involves creating new, modified relationships by altering the text of existing ones, ensuring that the associated entity mentions and predicted labels remain unchanged. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this augmentation method on four datasets, resulting in significant improvements in models' ability to recognize less common relationships. This technique can be applied to any relation extraction dataset and is available at https://github.com/allenai/data_aug_relation_extraction. We introduce a unified framework for the consumption of geometric structures across various deep learning systems. This framework consists of a collection of geometric objects, each corresponding to a particular type of deep learning model, along with a set of transformation rules that enable the seamless substitution of individual components. Furthermore, we provide a step-bygraph matching approach for the creation of custom geometric profiles from existing deep learning models. Our work encompasses a broad range of deep learning systems, including graph-based models, neural networks, and scoring functions, and is accompanied by a public repository containing detailed profiles of these models. By facilitating the exchange of knowledge across domains, our framework promotes the development of more efficient and effective deep learning models. This study delves into the use of expert variables in a deep neural network classifier for a jet substructure system known as YODA. YODA is a massless, jet-wide tagger that identifies boosted top quarks within hadronic events. By combining YODA with expert variables, the classifier can leverage additional information from the jet, enhancing its discrimination capabilities. We investigate the impact of incorporating sideboards, defined as small-radius sub-calculations of YODA, and topological characteristics like track and calorimeter measurements. Our analysis demonstrates that including these expert variables significantly improves the classifier's performance across various signal and background conditions. We examine the implementation of these sideboards in two scenarios: an idealized simulation and a real-world, experimentally-limited case. In both cases, the incorporation of expert variables yields a 10-30% improvement in discrimination, ultimately increasing the discovery potential for beyond-standard-model physics and optimizing the search for new physics in boosted top-quark decays. Our analysis provides a general framework for integrating expert variables into deep neural network classifiers in jet substructure systems. Additionally, we explore the use of expert variables in a complementary approach to YODA, which involves a mass-dependent analysis. This alternative method relies on expert variables to enhance its robustness and improve its ability to account for various uncertainties. Our findings indicate that expert variables enhance both YODA and its mass-dependent counterpart, underscoring their utility in a range of jet substructure applications. Our code and simulation data are publicly available on GitHub. https://github.com/alexjhall/YODA_experts.

A sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations occurs beyond half-filling in fermionic systems, severely hindering certain algorithm efficiency. To tackle this challenge, we've developed a novel worm algorithm addressing the sign issue. This approach involves introducing an auxiliary bias, which we eliminate through a related constraint using a maximally flat gauge technique derived from the level dynamics principle. This technique enables simulations of large systems with a high degree of precision without the limitations imposed by the sign problem, at any filling level. We've tested its effectiveness in the attractive Hubbard model, successfully extracting exact results for systems with three, four, and five sites. Furthermore, we've applied the technique to investigate dynamical correlation functions in larger systems, including those with lattice sizes of up to 32 sites. The results show excellent agreement with exact data, validating the technique's accuracy. This method provides a reliable solution to the sign problem, offering a promising approach for larger-scale simulations. The associated code is available on the repository https://github.com/MaxFlatGauge/worm-algorithm for review and modification purposes.

In a composite Higgs model featuring complex scalar fields, we explore the possibility of a parity-invariant symmetry group, $SO(6)/G$, with $G$ being $SU(3)$, analogous to the Flatto-M\"obius model. We then examine the consequences of a parity transformation that leaves the gauge group $SU(3)_L \otimes SU(3)_R$ invariant, selecting a parity-invariant set of chiral condensates. Subsequent analysis yields the linear sigma model Lagrangian and relevant perturbative and non-perturbative aspects. Ultimately, we discuss the possibility of a parity-invariant composite Higgs scenario. Additionally, we have made our calculations and derivations available online in an accompanying note. https://github.com/rodrigocosta/Parity-invariant-Composite-Higgs/tree/main/Code.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations (VPPMs) significantly enhances user interaction in virtual reality by creating a more natural and immersive experience. This study examines the effects of VPPMs on user presence in VR, employing a controlled experiment where participants' physiological responses and self-reported presence measures were recorded while interacting with a VR environment with or without VPPMs. The results indicate that the presence of VPPMs can have a significant positive impact, with specific benefits observed in the spatial awareness aspect of presence. This research provides insights into the optimal usage of VPPMs in VR applications to maximize user immersion. Furthermore, the study's findings can inform the development of more effective guidance systems for VPPMs to ensure a seamless transition from physical to virtual interactions. To expand a pre-trained multilingual model to accommodate new languages, we propose a technique called adaptive finetuning. This method involves adjusting the model's output layer to process additional languages without modifying its core parameters. We also introduce a data augmentation approach, called direction-specific backtranslation, which significantly enhances model performance for new languages by leveraging information from existing languages with similar directionality. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods, showing that our adaptive finetuning strategy outperforms comparable techniques by 4-6% across various transfer tasks, and our direction-specific backtranslation method surpasses random sampling approaches by 8-12% in new language adaptation. Furthermore, we develop a theoretical framework for analyzing adaptive finetuning and provide empirical guidance on its hyperparameter settings. Our code and model checkpoints are publicly available. Additionally, we establish a repository called AdapTL for tracking the latest advancements in adaptive finetuning and new language adaptation. This repository can be accessed at https://adaptl.github.io.

Social media has become a primary source of information, but it's also a breeding ground for misinformation. Current fact-checking methods mainly rely on manual processes, but they're insufficient to tackle the vast amount of content shared daily, especially on platforms that provide short-form videos and narratives. To overcome this limitation, we propose an automated system for fact-checking social media posts, combining techniques for gathering relevant information and establishing connections between disparate claims. Our approach yields promising results, outperforming existing methods in several datasets across multiple metrics. The system will be open-sourced, enabling future improvements through community collaboration.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time is crucial for various applications such as disaster response, sports analysis, and election monitoring. This requires not only detecting events but also filtering out irrelevant information like individual posts, thus focusing only on significant occurrences. This paper presents a novel approach to identify social media events using data streams and incorporates a new method to remove noise using context information. We evaluate this approach on two different datasets and compare it to existing techniques for comparative analysis. The results show that this approach outperforms traditional methods in terms of accuracy and event filtering. The implemented system is now available online for public use.

We've developed a weighted version of the skew-spectrum, a statistical tool that can be used to analyze cosmic structures and estimate key parameters. The weighted skew-spectrum is an extension of previously introduced methods for non-Gaussianity and anisotropy, allowing it to account for variations in volume and shot noise. We've demonstrated that this approach is highly resistant to changes in volume and shot noise, and has the potential to be a powerful low-order statistical measure for next-generation cosmological surveys. A simulation-based analysis was performed to assess the ability of the weighted skew-spectrum to constrain the equation of state of dark energy and the amplitude of scalar perturbations. The results indicate that this method can provide accurate estimates of these parameters, even in the presence of significant variations in volume and shot noise. Furthermore, we've found that the accuracy of the estimates can be significantly improved by including higher-order modes. The code used for this analysis is available online for public use. Additionally, we've outlined potential applications of the weighted skew-spectrum in the analysis of future cosmological surveys. These include its use in the analysis of data from the Roman Space Telescope, the Habitable Exoplanet Imaging Mission, and ground-based supernovae surveys. The weighted skew-spectrum may also be applicable to the analysis of data from gravitational wave lensing experiments, such as LISA. With its high sensitivity to non-Gaussianity and anisotropy, the weighted skew-spectrum has the potential to be a valuable tool in the analysis of a wide range of cosmological data. Future work will involve further developing the method to account for systematic biases and uncertainties. This will enable the use of the weighted skew-spectrum in the analysis of data from ongoing and future cosmological surveys. We introduce a novel approach to training Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) that can withstand a wide range of adversarial attacks by utilizing an ensemble of posterior samples. This method, known as Ensemble Maximum Likelihood Estimation (EML), generates robust BNNs capable of withstanding attacks such as PGD, AutoPGD, and Natural Adversarial Examples (NAE), outperforming current techniques in adversarial training. By integrating EML with Dirichlet Variational Inference (DVI) and a new regularization technique, we achieve state-of-the-art results in adversarial training, particularly on CIFAR-10 with a simple MNIST-like dataset configuration. Our research demonstrates that BNNs can be robust to diverse adversarial attacks by utilizing multiple network models, and provides open-source code for replication.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to a public health crisis and a surge in online misinformation. This study investigates the spread of online rumors in China regarding COVID-19. Our analysis of 338 rumors and his retention in Chinese social media reveals that these rumors primarily originated from health-related information gaps and were fueled by the desire for novelty. We observed that the diffusion of these rumors follows a non-normal distribution pattern and can be predicted using the Bradley-Terry-Sarlev model. Additionally, our results indicate that the spread of rumors is influenced by their breaking news value and the characteristics of social media users. Based on these findings, we provide data-driven recommendations for mitigating the spread of COVID-19-related rumors on social media. Our study's insights can be applied to other public health emergencies and social media platforms. A publicly available R package, RumorMetrics, has been developed to facilitate the replication of our analysis. It includes functions for data preprocessing, network analysis, rumor characterization, and the estimation of diffusion patterns and spread likelihood. This research investigates the effects of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. It compares the performance of different dimensionality reduction techniques, such as PCA, MMSE, and random projection, across a range of compression rates and datasets. Our findings reveal that some methods excel at specific compression rates, yet degrade elsewhere, making it essential to optimize dimensionality reduction to dataset and classification model specifications. Additionally, we introduce a straightforward approach to selecting the ideal compression rate and dimensionality reduction method on a per-pixel basis. Our proposed method utilizes a nearest neighbor classifier and demonstrates improved accuracy across various datasets. Notably, our results indicate that random projection can be a reliable and computationally efficient option for hyperspectral pixel classification. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/alexeyguz/hyperspectral_dimensionality_reduction.

Deep neural networks are highly effective in various applications but require substantial computational resources for training and inference. The lottery ticket hypothesis proposes that a neural network's training can be viewed as a weight pruning process that identifies efficacious sub-networks. Building upon this idea, this study presents a novel approach, layer-level ticket training, which enables the discovery of useful sub-networks within specific layers. Our method involves incorporating additional constraints during training for identifying efficacious sub-networks at the layer level. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach yields high accuracy when testing sub-networks composed of only convolutional layers, and we also show the method's applicability to other pruning methods as comparative examples. Furthermore, we successfully employed our approach to uncover efficacious sub-networks in ResNet-50 for image classification and MobileNetV2 for mobile inference. Notably, our method allows the retrieval of a 97% accurate sub-network in ResNet-50 with only 0.8% of the original weights. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyu-1999/LayerTT.git.

Deep neural networks are highly effective supervised classifiers that can be optimized using a variety of loss functions. While there is no universally optimal loss function, cross-entropy has become the de facto standard due to its efficient mathematical properties. However, the choice of loss function is often overlooked in deep learning, leading to potential improvements being neglected. In this study, a comprehensive examination of loss function behavior is conducted, analyzing how it influences both training and generalization. A new loss function, the hyperbolic cross-entropy, is proposed and demonstrated to enhance generalization performance in specific scenarios. Additionally, the study provides insights into the relationship between loss function and generalizability, offering valuable guidance for deep learning practitioners. The findings are validated through a range of experiments involving various network architectures, datasets, and loss functions, shedding light on their underlying dynamics. The code is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/alexeyguz/hyperbolic-cross-entropy.

In systems for community safety reporting, 911 call centers dispatch personnel who provide emotional support to individuals in need. While the effectiveness of in-person emotional support is well-documented, its impact via phone is less understood. To fill this knowledge gap, we conducted a study involving over 300,000 community safety reports and found that when dispatchers provided emotional support, the number of follow-up reports increased substantially. Notably, this benefit was particularly significant for reports submitted by users who were already experiencing high levels of distress. Furthermore, we discovered that dispatchers' emotional support had a more pronounced effect when they used more supportive language. To take a deeper look into these interactions, we developed a system that automatically detects instances of emotional support and connects it to subsequent system outcomes. Our research provides a foundation for further exploring the role of emotional support in community safety reporting and highlights opportunities for improvement in existing systems. With continued data collection, we anticipate that our findings will become even more accurate and generalizable. Ultimately, this research may lead to the development of new methods for providing emotional support via phone. To analyze superconductivity in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with a surface spin-orbit coupling modified by a gate, we investigate the superconducting properties of a quantum wire made from this material. Within a model that accounts for both spin and orbital effects using a 2D superconducting wave function, we find that gate-induced spin-orbit coupling results in a unique phase shift. Consequently, the superconducting gap exhibits asymmetry and becomes dependent on the wire's direction, ultimately leading to a transition from a $p$-wave to an $s$-wave superconducting state as the gate coupling strength increases. Notably, this transition exhibits non-monotonic behavior when influenced by real-world disorder. Our research provides a theoretical framework for understanding superconducting properties in gate-modulated topological insulators. Moreover, we suggest that magnetoelectrical transport measurements in these materials can serve as a test of our theoretical predictions. Specifically, we propose that Bi$_2$Se$_3$ thin films with a non-uniform gate coverage could display diverse phases, including both $p$-wave and $s$-wave superconductivity. Furthermore, we predict that the half-group-conjugate Cooper pair channel could be active in these materials, making them detectable through specific measurements. Active learning techniques prompt humans to label uncertain samples, but current approaches fall into two limited strategies: utilizing model uncertainty or relying on subset selection methods. We introduce a new approach that leverages graph diffusion to actively choose data points for labeling. This method, called Active Graph Learning, connects nodes during the pre-training phase and exploits the resulting graph structure to select highly connected data points for human annotation. Our experiments show AGL outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significant margins across various datasets and settings. Additionally, we've open-sourced our code to facilitate further research in this area.

To investigate the evolution of rock music's dynamic characteristics, we analyzed data from the Million Song Dataset, calculating the standard metrics of loudness and tempo for songs from the 1960s to the 2000s. Notably, our research revealed a significant increase in the complexity of songs over time, with the standard deviation of loudness growing by 20% since the 1960s. To gain deeper insights, we developed a mathematical model to simulate the evolution of a musical population, where artists and record labels strive to optimize their creative decisions to maximize profits. Our model showed that the increasing complexity of rock music is an unintended consequence of these optimization efforts, which can be observed in a theoretical phase diagram. Additionally, our model's predictions on song popularity and the distribution of loudness and tempo align with empirical data. Our study provides a theoretical explanation for the observed evolution of rock music's dynamic characteristics. Furthermore, our model offers a framework for analyzing the co-evolution of interconnected musical attributes. Lastly, our research highlights the potential for phase diagrams to capture the general trends in cultural evolution. We analyze the behavior of a stochastic process where numbers are added to a group of blocks over time. The system starts with a single-element group and as each number is added, it either joins an existing block with a probability governed by a decreasing function of the block size, or creates a new block. We investigate the distribution of block sizes as time progresses and show that under a specific condition on the function, the resulting distribution approaches a stable, self-repeating pattern that does not depend on the initial group configuration. This repeating pattern is analogous to a fractal, exhibiting repeating patterns within itself. We also identify a condition on the function that ensures the system converges to a single, unique block containing all added numbers. The condition for this convergence is that the pattern repeats quickly enough, specifically at an exponential rate, and we show that the system converges to a single block if the function decreases rapidly enough. The rate of convergence is independent of the system's starting point and we provide a precise estimate of how quickly the system converges to the single-block state. The analysis relies on a complex mathematical approach, utilizing Markov process theory and the concept of regeneration in stochastic processes. This work presents an intuitionistic natural deduction system, called NDinv, which provides a formalization of the inversion property traditionally proven by structural induction. NDinv is derived from a more fundamental calculus, called NDinv0, that incorporates only essential properties of intuitionistic logic. By encoding NDinv0 in a typed lambda calculus, we demonstrate that the inversion property is explicitly expressible within this encoding, thereby providing a theoretical basis for its proof rather than requiring structural induction. Additionally, we examine the relationship between NDinv and other inversion-based proof systems for intuitionistic logic. Notably, we show that the proofs generated by NDinv are equivalent to those produced by the S4EC calculus of Belnap and Montagna. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of adapting NDinv to model classical logic by incorporating a negation operator that satisfies a preconceived notion of behavior. This adaptation is inspired by the classical natural deduction system of Heyting and Prawitz. Finally, we examine the possibility of applying NDinv to provide a formalization of the proof-theoretic behavior of negation in natural deduction, specifically in relation to cut-elimination and the propositional calculus. This investigation is motivated by the similarity between the inversions performed in NDinv and the reductions carried out in the cut-elimination procedure. Specifically, we consider the inversions as a form of reverse reduction, and we propose that the inversions of all instances of a given formula be seen as a collective reverse reduction of that formula. This idea is analogous to the concept of overwriting in the focus calculus of Girard. This study is an expanded version of the author's conference paper. model that leverages human feedback with relative and absolute confidence levels.

current state-of-the-art methods in image classification and visual retrieval tasks

We establish that a topological space's local compactness is equivalent to its Smyth powerspace being core-compact. Upon finding that upper powersets do not possess a core-compact Smyth powerspace for any non-trivial topological space, we deduce that local compactness is the sole topological property that imitates core-compactness in Smyth powerspaces. This paper presents a novel machine learning estimator, the grouped AIPW, which builds upon existing work by VanderWeele and Vansteelandt in 2017 and further generalizes the result of Li, Liang and Zhou in 2020. We demonstrate that the new estimator maintains key characteristics of both the AIPW and nAIPW estimators. A significant outcome of this research is the development of an asymptotic linear theory, which justifies the performance of the grouped AIPW in a variety of applications. We also conduct simulations to assess the estimator's efficacy. Furthermore, the theoretical results are utilized to examine the bias and variance of the grouped AIPW in specific scenarios. Ultimately, the estimator is applied to estimate a direct causal effect in the presence of grouped confounders. We derive asymptotic distributions for the estimator and its variance, which enables the development of test statistics and critical values for assessing causal relationships. The research culminates in an empirical analysis of the effect of air pollution on infant mortality using the grouped AIPW estimator. We find strong evidence supporting a positive relationship between air pollution and infant mortality. The associated R code can be found at https://github.com/stephengriffin/grouped_aipw. Artificial molecular motors, powered by electric fields, operate through a combination of field-induced torque and breakdown of their symmetry. This influence of electric currents can be likened to the in-flight orientation of meteorites in the Earth's gravitational field. A theoretical framework has been developed to study the dynamics of these motors in solution, taking into account their shape, electric field, Brownian motion, and electrostatic forces. This approach is applied to a specific motor made of a DNA double helix and small cation molecules, which shows that its movement is largely determined by the motor's initial state and the electric field strength. This research provides a deeper understanding of the motor's behavior and identifies the factors that influence its rotation. Additionally, it is shown that the motor can be made to rotate in a specific direction by adjusting the electric field and the length of the DNA double helix. This study has significant implications for the development of more complex molecular machines powered by electric fields. This paper investigates the computational feasibility of the $\ell_2$-Stein Discrepancy, a statistical measure used to assess the uniqueness of solutions. We demonstrate that computing the $\ell_2$-Stein Discrepancy for two arbitrary functions of size $n$ requires at least $O(n^2)$ time complexity. A more efficient algorithm is proposed, achieving $O(n \log n)$ time complexity. The functions in question are assumed to be represented by their values at grid points. The algorithm first constructs a matrix representing the function values at grid points, then applies the Sherman-Morrison Woodbury formula to obtain the desired outcome. The proposed method is subsequently applied to $\ell_2$-Stein Discrepancy in various applications, including Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, statistical inference, and generative modeling. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world data show that the algorithm significantly outperforms the naive approach. It is also compared to an existing method that is not directly applicable to functions of size $n$. The code for the algorithm is available online at https://github.com/kuwahashi/stein_discrepancy. The discovery of GJ 229B in 1995 as the first directly imaged exoplanet in our solar system marked a significant turning point in the field of exoplanetary science. Initially classified as a Jupiter-like planet, recent reanalysis using outdated spectroscopic data yielded a surprisingly low mass for the companion of just 27 Earth masses. We have conducted new high-precision spectroscopic retrievals using high-quality spectra from multiple datasets, including data collected by the HIRES instrument at the Keck Observatory. Our analysis indicates that GJ 229B has a mass of approximately 47.3 Jupiter masses at a distance of 0.121 AU and an effective temperature of around 620 K. These findings align with theoretical models suggesting that GJ 229B is likely a super-Jupiter or a brown dwarf. The discovery of GJ 229B has provided valuable insights into the formation of planetary systems, and its unique characteristics make it an essential target for further study in the field of exoplanetary science. Additionally, we have developed a model to describe the atmospheric properties of the system and its substellar companion, which will be presented in a future publication. To meet diverse wireless applications needs, cellular networks have implemented different spectrum bands. However, these networks often fall short in providing licensed spectrum to meet the demands of several wireless applications. Consequently, numerous applications require more licensed spectrum than what is available through traditional cellular networks. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach that enables efficient sharing of licensed spectrum among different wireless applications. Specifically, we develop a two-stage framework to optimize licensed spectrum allocation for coexisting wireless applications. In the first stage, we identify the available licensed spectrum within each base station using an iterative approach that maximizes their individual revenues. Subsequently, we allocate licensed spectrum to various wireless applications at their terminals through a graph coloring technique to ensure maximum base station revenue. Our proposed framework is evaluated using real-world data and demonstrated to effectively increase the revenue generated by each base station and wireless application. Furthermore, we analyze the computational complexity of our approach. Notably, we observed that the revenue generated by our framework is significantly closer to the optimal value, achieving an average deviation of less than 1%. Our approach also offers improved revenue to base stations and wireless applications, with average increases of 26% and 35%, respectively. Our results indicate that our framework is a practical and efficient solution for licensed spectrum allocation. Furthermore, we verified the effectiveness of our approach by conducting simulations under different scenarios, including varying numbers of coexisting wireless applications and base stations. Our results show that our framework is adaptable to different operational conditions and spectrum availability. Our approach is also compared to a heuristic method that allocates licensed spectrum based on application priority, yielding improved results in 57% of the tested scenarios. Our framework offers a more efficient solution, with a computational complexity of O(n^3), compared to the heuristic method's complexity of O(n^5). Our work contributes to the body of knowledge by introducing a novel approach to licensed spectrum allocation, thereby enhancing the revenue generated by base stations and wireless applications. Our results provide insights into the effectiveness of our framework under different operational conditions, offering a framework for future research in this domain. The DTW distance is a prominent measure for comparing time series, but its computation can be costly due to its O(N-D) time complexity, where N and D represent the series lengths and a predefined threshold. Advanced variants like EAPrunedDTW efficiently reduce DTW's time complexity to O(d) in advance, where d is the minimum possible distance. This algorithm works by establishing upper bounds for DTW distances, thus eliminating unnecessary computations. In this study, we enhance EAPrunedDTW by introducing a more efficient upper bound calculation, significantly reducing required memory to 3d from 5d previously. Additionally, we present a new approach to obtain the DTW distance directly from these upper bounds without further refinement. Experimental results on diverse datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art implementation of EAPrunedDTW. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/CompDataSci/EAPrunedDTW.

Over-smoothing is a significant issue in Graph Convolutional Networks, causing them to converge to identical representations regardless of the graph structure. This occurs due to successive applications of graph convolution layers, leading to performance degradation unless prevented by residual connections or graph normalization. In this research, we introduce the concept of over-smoothing and common countermeasures for Graph Convolutional Neural Networks, before proposing a novel approach based on eigendecomposition to counter over-smoothing. Our method, which utilizes eigenvalues to determine the risk of over-smoothing, can be applied to various graph convolution architectures and networks, including those with non-symmetric graphs. Furthermore, we examine the effects of eigenvector multiplication on representation loss and demonstrate our approach to be a feasible solution to prevent over-smoothing. Our proposed method is then evaluated on several benchmark datasets, yielding state-of-the-art results for semi-supervised node classification. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenXu1998/Over-Smoothing-Prevention-by-Eigendecomposition.

To answer this question, we conducted an experiment involving a first-price auction with fully and partially informed buyers and sellers. Our findings indicate that when buyers' beliefs about the auction format do not align with reality, they tend to overpay and our designed mechanism fails to achieve efficiency. Notably, the discrepancy in beliefs does not significantly impact the earnings of fully informed agents. To address this issue, we introduced a simple correction method that relies solely on aggregate data and is shown to effectively mitigate the credibility problem, leading to a significant improvement in buyers' gains. Furthermore, this approach has the added benefit of being resistant to bidder manipulation. Our research provides a novel application of Cramér's theorem in the context of auctions and contributes to the existing literature on credibility in auctions. Additionally, we used agent-based models to gain insights into the behavior of more complex bidder types and the potential impact of credibility on their earnings. Our results suggest that credibility can have a substantial effect on the earnings of strategic bidder types, including snipebidders and second-price auction optimizers. To facilitate the use of credibility-corrected data in real-world auctions, we developed a straightforward procedure that can be employed by auctioneers to assess the credibility of auction formats and identify potential biases. Our research provides a significant advancement in the understanding of credibility in auctions and has practical implications for both researchers and practitioners. Specifically, our findings can guide the design of credible auction formats and inform bidders on how to make strategic decisions in the presence of credibility issues. Furthermore, our study can aid auctioneers in identifying and mitigating potential credibility problems that may arise during the operation of an auction. To effectively utilize academic papers, Question Answering systems need to accurately extract relevant information. Current systems, however, struggle to interpret sentences beyond their word-level connections. This limitation stems from a lack of deep contextual understanding, which is due in part to the absence of suitable datasets requiring multi-hop reasoning. To address this, we've developed DeepRead-QA, a dataset consisting of 1,167 questions that require the analysis of multiple sentences across 434 passages from 121 scientific papers. We've also created DeepRead-Retriever, a data-driven retriever that leverages sentence embeddings to identify relevant passages. By integrating DeepRead-Retriever with DeepRead-QA, we've achieved state-of-the-art results on the Natural Questions dataset and demonstrated superior generalizability on strong baselines. The dataset and implementation are publicly available at https://github.com/allenai/DeepRead-QA.

We investigated neutrino flavor instability within the context of core-collapse supernovae using the ONeMg 15-to-25 solar mass star model. This model was chosen due to its potential for fast instability in neutrino flavors, which poses significant challenges for numerical simulations. We conducted a series of supernova simulations, varying factors that contribute to instability, including the mass of the progenitor, neutrino opacities, and energy yields from the neutron star surface. Our findings indicate that fast instability is prevalent across a broad mass range, specifically within 0.4-10 solar masses, particularly in regions near the core. We observed significant differences in instability compared to a standard case with 18 solar mass progenitor and standard neutrino opacities. Notably, we found that increasing neutrino opacities by a factor of 10 eliminated the instability. Furthermore, we found that higher energy yields from the neutron star surface enhanced instability, while reducing the mass of the progenitor within our study range had a minor effect. Our results suggest that fast instability in supernovae simulations is a widespread phenomenon, particularly in massive neutron star models. We also found that precision in flavor oscillation predictions can be achieved by adjusting neutrino emission parameters, which could be an alternative to modifying the standard theory. Our study provides new insights into the behavior of neutrino flavor instability in supernovae and paves the way for further research into this phenomenon. We also present a new method for analyzing instability in supernovae simulations, which can be applied to a wide range of cases. Our code and analysis are available for public use. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, affecting both children and adults, is a complex condition difficult to detect accurately. Current diagnostic methods are often unreliable and expensive. Research into using machine learning to identify ADHD from brain scans has shown promise, but most studies have focused on the entire brain. We investigated whether a deep learning model could identify ADHD using only specific areas of interest, reducing computational costs and simplifying interpretation. Our results show that a model using 56 selected regions outperformed one using the entire brain in 302 subjects. Furthermore, we identified the most crucial regions for the model's accuracy. To verify these findings, we conducted cross-validation and tested the model's performance on an independent dataset, achieving a 75.8% accuracy rate. These outcomes support the use of a compact, efficient, and interpretable model for identifying ADHD. We also discovered that ADHD could be differentiated from healthy controls using a one-class SVM trained on the selected areas. This research provides a reliable and efficient approach to identifying ADHD. We have made our code and data available for other researchers. Acronyms are shortened versions of written expressions, often used as a time-saving method, but their ambiguity can lead to comprehension difficulties in written texts. To resolve this, a system has been proposed that learns to predict acronym expansions automatically. Based on the assumption that acronym expansions are typically phrases consisting of one or two words, a system was developed to estimate acronym expansions by generating candidate phrases and ranking them according to relevance. Experimental results demonstrate the system's effectiveness in a large-scale dataset containing 1 million articles. Notably, the system outperforms a similar approach presented in a previous study. A publicly accessible tool allows researchers to replicate the findings and evaluate the proposed method. In oscillatory media, pacemaker centers can give rise to traveling waves of increased activity that spread throughout the system. This study investigates how these waves of activity, triggered by the pacemaker, impact synchronization within the system. We employed a model of coupled chaotic circuits to represent a oscillatory medium interconnecting two pacemaker circuits and analyzed the effects of activity waves on the system's overall synchronization. Our findings indicate that these waves can either enhance or diminish synchronization within the system, contingent upon specific system parameters. Notably, this phenomenon is associated with a particular type of instability in the system, where small disturbances can cause activity waves to emerge. We also observed that, in systems with a unidirectional connection configuration, these activity waves can cause synchronized patterns to emerge, even if the system was not initially set up to exhibit such patterns. This research sheds new light on the complex interplay between activity waves and synchronization in oscillatory systems. Further investigation into this phenomenon could provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of activity propagation within living systems. Additionally, this study's findings could be applied to improve the design of medical devices, such as pacemakers, by better understanding the effects of their generated signals on the heart's overall functioning. This knowledge could also be utilized to develop new methods for inducing synchronized activity in oscillatory systems, which could have various practical applications in medicine and science. system is a crucial task but faces challenges due to the limited availability and
quality of annotated data in several languages, particularly Chinese. To overcome
this limitation, we developed a data enhancement method that utilizes large-scale
unlabeled Chinese medical discharge summaries to improve the accuracy of ICD
coding. Our method employs a pre-trained transformer model to predict ICD codes
based on the selected medical discharge summary segments, outperforming current
state-of-the-art Chinese medical record encoding models. Additionally, we
introduce the Chinese Medical Record Encoding Task to provide a comprehensive
evaluation framework that assesses encoding models using multiple document
types, thereby facilitating further research in this area. Our model and data
can be accessed at https://github.com/zhengyizhao/cmre.
