We've developed a new method to identify microlensing planets that use data from the 2020 and 2021 seasons of the Global Network of Automated Telescope, consisting of time-series data from 13 telescopes in the prime field. This area received extensive attention from the Gaia mission, enabling us to cross-reference the data and pinpoint potential locations of these planets. Our approach utilizes a neural network to analyze microlensing anomalies and accurately detects them, outperforming the initial analysis. By integrating parallax information, we've successfully identified two new prime-field microlensing planets, including one with a unique and minimal mass. Our research also presents a comprehensive analysis of the prime field's planetary system, including data on detected microlensing events and their potential to host planets. This study showcases the effectiveness of combining ground-based and space-based data to identify celestial bodies. Additionally, the code and data used in this research are freely accessible.

Differentiable rendering has become a key component in addressing image-based inverse problems by linking the process of rendering objects with solving image tasks. We have developed an innovative method for differentiable mesh rendering that utilizes rasterization for high-speed and high-quality output. Our method transforms the challenge of generating meshes into optimizing control points, achieving this optimization through a novel connection between rasterization and implicit functions. This advancement empowers complex image editing tasks such as changing object shapes, scenes with multiple objects, and restoring damaged images. Our results demonstrate exceptional quality and accuracy in these tasks. Additionally, our method provides high-quality, artifact-free outputs in a fraction of the time required by other approaches. For instance, it takes only 0.3 seconds to edit a 10k triangle mesh. Our code and demo are publicly available.

This research introduces a novel approach to estimating the variance in traffic conditions for specific routes and times within a larger network of roads. The method utilizes data from floating car sensors, accounting for the limited number of detectors by factoring in the spatial correlations of traffic variability. By applying this, network managers can identify periods and areas of high traffic uncertainty, ultimately enabling more accurate forecasting and routing decisions. The proposed method is subsequently demonstrated on a real-world road network in Beijing, China. Results show that it effectively pinpoints locations and times of elevated traffic uncertainty, providing valuable insights that could guide decision-making in traffic management. The method is shown to outperform a simpler alternative that models variance independently at each detector location. The proposed method is further expandable to accommodate additional types of sensor data not considered in this particular study. The associated code is publicly available on the repository https://github.com/zhengyizhao/VarCorr.

The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees by generating uniform random spanning trees through repeated random walks. We examine the probability that these algorithms are still generating uniform spanning trees after an arbitrary number of steps, say step $N$. On a fixed graph with $L$ vertices, the probability that the Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms remain uniform at step $N$ can be expressed in terms of the number of $k$-dominating sets of size $k$ on the graph, where $k\leq L$. This study introduces SenNA, a semantic network navigator assistant that utilizes 
word embeddings to enhance linked data entity exploration through natural language 
interfaces. SenNA employs pre-trained distributional semantic models to map 
natural language phrases and understand user queries. It leverages these mapped 
concepts to identify relevant entities in the linked data, which are then displayed 
to the user in a visual network. To support non-expert users, SenNA includes a 
simplified query interface that provides essential RDFS properties and a set of basic 
predefined search options. Furthermore, SenNA incorporates a dynamic entity 
suggestion feature to assist users in formulating their queries. Comprehensive 
evaluations have demonstrated SenNA's effectiveness in balancing user support and 
data coverage. SenNA is currently accessible at senna.semanticweb.org. Additionally, 
the source code is freely available on GitHub at github.com/semanticwebSWE/Senna.

systems. To facilitate this process, guidance techniques are employed by the

This study compares the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods in solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the heart's deformation under different loads, the problem becomes a nonlinear system that is typically solved using the Newton-Raphson method. However, this approach often leads to large nonlinear systems that are computationally expensive to solve. To overcome this issue, an interface solver is used within a BDDC method, while the corresponding solvers on individual sub-domains are employed in the AMG comparison. The research involves analyzing the impact of different grid finite elements on the solvers' performance and presents a detailed study on the construction of the interface solver. Extensive numerical results demonstrate the relationship between the solvers' performance and the characteristics of the grid finite elements. The BDDC method consistently outperforms the AMG method in terms of computational efficiency, but the difference is particularly noticeable on finer grids. The research also highlights the potential of the BDDC method as a suitable choice for solving cardiac mechanics problems. Bianisotropic acoustic metagratings are highly versatile elements with various 
applications in the transmission of plane waves. However, their use in the 
reflection of plane waves is largely unexplored. In this study, we introduce a 
theory and design method for a new type of acoustic isolator based on 
bianisotropic metagratings. We utilize a generalized acoustic wave scattering 
problem to establish a rigorous relationship between the reflection phase and 
surface characteristics. A genetic algorithm is then employed to optimize the 
element's structure for maximum reflection isolation. Numerical simulations 
validate our theoretical framework and the effectiveness of the designed 
structures in the transmission of plane waves. Moreover, we demonstrate the 
potential of these acoustic isolators in the context of real-time ultrasound 
image reconstruction. Ultimately, our findings provide a foundation for the 
development of novel acoustic devices with unique properties.

Current reinforcement learning solutions are predominantly designed for closed-world environments. However, when adapted to open-world settings, they often struggle with poor generalization to unfamiliar situations. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework that leverages the diversity of experiences to improve policy performance. Our approach utilizes a population of agents to explore different states and policies, and assigns weights to experiences based on their predictive value for the agent population. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through successful applications in two challenging domains: a sparsely rewarding level design system and a dynamic, ever-expanding game of cross-domain navigation. Our results show that our method achieves better performance than existing approaches in these domains. Additionally, we provide theoretical justifications for the experiences weights and the benefits of multi-agent diversity. Our framework and associated datasets are available online at: https://github.com/alexrame/Experience_Weighting.

We have made our code available to the community for further research and development.

Urban hyperspectral images offer detailed information about various city elements, allowing precise segmentation. However, their high-dimensional nature and limited availability make them challenging to work with. We address these challenges by introducing a multi-scale hyperspectral segmentation approach that leverages a pixel-wise sparse prior to filter out irrelevant data and focus on city features. A network is then trained to derive high-resolution hyperspectral images from lower-resolution ones and combine them with a hyperspectral prior to produce accurate results. A novel loss function is developed to minimize color and spatial differences between predicted and ground-truth segments. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in hyperspectral semantic segmentation. The code is available at https://github.com/zhenghui-ai/MHSS.

Observations of the rotation rates of the low-mass giant stars in the Kepler field reveal a discrepancy - their cores rotate significantly faster than their surfaces. This discrepancy can be attributed to a redistribution of angular momentum due to internal waves and/or a change in the structure of the stars. currently supports optimizing applications with iterative, polyphase, and 
unrolling-based iterative workflows, as well as operator-level optimization. The 
library has been used in optimizing applications such as ResNet50 and MobileNet, 
and has demonstrated significant performance improvements when combined with 
hardware-specific techniques like data packing and quantization. LibOPT's source 
code and a set of pre-built binaries are available for download on GitHub. A 
detailed user guide and API documentation can also be found on the GitHub page.

------------------------

LibOPT has been used to optimize several applications, including image 
classification, object detection, and video analysis. The following are some of 
the performance results: 

- Image classification: LibOPT has achieved performance improvements of up to 34x 
over CPU performance when running on FPGAs, and up to 4x over CPU performance 
when running on GPUs. 

- Object detection: LibOPT has achieved performance improvements of up to 26x 
over CPU performance when running on FPGAs, and up to 3x over CPU performance 
when running on GPUs. 

- Video analysis: LibOPT has achieved performance improvements of up to 22x 
over CPU performance when running on FPGAs, and up to 2x over CPU performance 
when running on GPUs.

This paper presents a navigation system for a mobile robotic arm that generates collision-free paths by integrating obstacle avoidance techniques. Envisioned as a robotic surgery platform, the robotic arm must move efficiently through tight spaces while maintaining a safe distance from its surroundings. Our approach utilizes a planning module based on the Reeds-Sheap algorithm, combining heuristics for the arm's movement and a set of predefined safety constraints. To optimize performance, we developed an evaluation function that prioritizes nearest points and closest targets, allowing the arm to move more quickly along the planned path. Experimental results show significant reductions in computation time without sacrificing safety. Compared to the original system, our approach yields a 30% improvement in speed while maintaining a 99% success rate in avoiding obstacles. Furthermore, we successfully tested our method in a realistic, high-occupancy surgical environment, achieving a 100% success rate. Our findings indicate that this navigation system can effectively support robotic surgery in complex environments. To validate our solution, we conducted thorough comparisons with other approaches, demonstrating its superior performance in related research. Pulsar halos are large, diffuse structures formed from the synchrotron radiation of high-energy electrons, which can serve as indicators of cosmic-ray propagation in the Galaxy. A comprehensive study of 12 pulsar halos was conducted to examine their connection to nearby pulsars and potential sources of cosmic rays. By analyzing their positions and sizes, researchers found that halos are primarily associated with young pulsars that have not yet slowed down. However, a minority of pulsars, including PSR J1057$+$4526, exhibit high speeds, suggesting that they may have been formed through interactions with the Galaxy's central molecular disk. Furthermore, the study discovered a correlation between the distance of halos from their associated pulsars and the pulsar's velocity, which could be explained by the influence of the Galaxy's magnetic field. This research provides new insights into the relationship between pulsar halos, high-energy electrons, and the Galaxy's magnetic field. A statistical analysis of the sizes and brightness of pulsar halos also revealed a connection to the surrounding density of cosmic-ray sources, which could be used to develop more accurate models of cosmic-ray propagation in the Galaxy. We introduce the RFS Dataset, an open collection of radar images and signals designed to advance Fully Polarimetric Radar Image Segmentation capabilities. The dataset comprises 1000 images, categorized into five weather types - clear sky, light rain, heavy rain, snow, and hail - obtained from a mobile radar system. The dataset is unique due to its self-collected data, obtained through concurrent radar measurements and video recordings of the sky. The RFS Dataset serves as a benchmark for evaluating FPRIS methods, with existing ones demonstrated to require significant tuning on a single dataset. The implementation details, including dataset access, are available at https://rfsdataset.github.io/.

Climate change is a pressing global issue that has been receiving varying levels of public attention across different regions and time periods.  Between 2007-2017, a survey involving over 9,500 individuals in over 15 European and North American countries measured public awareness and understanding of climate science.  These data were then used to create a climate index, which showed significant fluctuations in public interest, ranging from a 25% increase in interest among German respondents to a 20% decrease in interest among US respondents.  Variations in public interest were linked to factors such as media coverage, government policies, and local weather events, rather than differences in climate education.  These findings highlight the importance of understanding the dynamic relationship between climate knowledge and public behavior.  Furthermore, they suggest that educational interventions may have a more significant impact when combined with other strategies to influence public opinion.  Finally, they underscore the need for policy-makers to be aware of how public opinion is shaped by external factors. Recent studies have demonstrated the potential for analyzing cosmological density perturbations through quasar spectra by utilizing machine learning techniques to identify specific absorption features. We have developed a new approach to achieve this using a neural network-based method, applying it to a simulation of a MgII absorption feature with varying amplitudes of linear and non-linear perturbations along the line of sight. By training our model to distinguish between linear and non-linear perturbations, we were able to accurately classify data with amplitudes less than 10% of the non-linear range, achieving a 99% success rate. Furthermore, we were able to estimate the ratio of non-linear to linear perturbations with a 5% margin of error. This method demonstrates a promising future for analyzing cosmological density perturbations through quasar spectra, potentially providing new insights into the structure and evolution of the universe.

Let 𝕙 be a semisimple Lie algebra over a field 𝔽 of characteristic zero, and U(𝕙) be its universal enveloping algebra. We consider tensor products of quasi-finite highest weight modules and U(𝕙)-free modules. Our main finding shows that under specific conditions, these tensor products are irreducible. We also establish a characterization of irreducible U(𝕙)-free modules, which are generated by one-dimensional 𝔽[𝕙]-modules. Furthermore, we compute the braiding on the category of U(𝕙)-free 𝔽[𝕙]-modules generated by one-dimensional 𝔽[𝕙]-modules. Our study also includes a specific examination of type A n−1 Lie algebras. The results provided are extensions of earlier research by Kashiwara and Ben-Zvi et al. on similar topics. Our proof methods involve the use of combinatorial techniques, similar to those employed in the study of Fock spaces in type A n−1 Lie algebras. Our findings are presented in a manner that is accessible to both Lie algebra and combinatorial specialists. The study is concluded with a potential generalization to type B n−1 and D n Lie algebras. Recent approaches like Self-Attention, GRU, and CSR have achieved significant success in this domain. This research introduces a theoretical model for resistive switching at the molecular level, utilizing assemblies under 10nm in length that can withstand high voltages. We focus on a single-component system, consisting of monovalent metal atoms, and demonstrate that electrostatic forces can induce a transition between two stable states with high energy barriers. This is achieved through the movement of a metal atom within a nanotube, resulting in a switch from a high-conductivity state with a metal atom and two electrons to a low-conductivity state with a metal atom and no additional electrons. Our findings show that even small systems can sustain high voltages, and that energy efficiency can be improved by incorporating a heat source. We also examine the possibility of thermal activation and predict that switching rates could reach 100 MHz with moderate temperatures. This theoretical model provides a framework for the design of efficient, small-scale resistive switching systems. Additionally, we have made the source code for the simulations available.

Transition-metal oxides in a thin film state can exhibit unique properties 
different from their bulk counterparts. When these films are a few atoms thick, 
they can easily bond with a single layer of donor material to form a 
two-dimensional composite. This composite can display a metallic behavior, 
causing an overlap of electron energy levels. Our study focuses on the energy 
bands of ultra-thin strontium vanadate, utilizing x-ray photoemission spectroscopy 
and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy to analyze electron behavior. 
Results indicate that this composite is an ultra-thin metal, with two-dimensional 
properties dominating its behavior. This is further supported by the 
temperature-dependent changes in its energy bands, influenced by quantum 
uncertainty and electron interaction. Ultimately, our findings provide a basis 
for understanding the properties of ultra-thin metal oxides in a two-dimensional 
environment. Additionally, our research can contribute to the development of 
two-dimensional oxides with potential in spintronics and other advanced fields.

This research examines the interconnectedness within cryptocurrency markets using a high-resolution approach that analyzes cross-membrane interactions. Our findings reveal that stablecoins play a central role in these networks from a statistical perspective, prioritizing them over other cryptocurrencies. By focusing on a cryptocurrency's order book data, our model captures the collective behavior of market participants and their impact on price, similar to the study of complex biological systems. The resulting networks are composed of components that represent price movements and interconnections demonstrating how market participants interact at the micro-scale. Utilizing standardized metrics, we investigate the structural and functional properties of individual cryptocurrencies and the cryptocurrency market as a whole. Our analysis provides a detailed understanding of each cryptocurrency's significance and contribution to the network. Our results show that stablecoins maintain central positions despite changes in the network's structure and function over time. Our study's approach can be applied to other financial systems and offers a new perspective on high-frequency financial data. The code used for this research is publicly available on GitHub. https://github.com/andersonmarchesani/CrossMem-Crypto.

In the realm of deep learning, complexity is often viewed through the lens of model size or its equivalent parameter count. However, this perspective overlooks the inherent structural organization within deep neural networks, which can be more effectively captured by their geometric complexity. This paper introduces a quantitative measure of geometric complexity that enables the comparison of deep learning models based on their internal architecture. This novel metric is then employed to investigate the connection between geometric complexity and generalization performance in deep neural networks. The resulting findings indicate that geometric complexity serves as a more effective predictor of generalization than parameter count, while also revealing its relationship with task-specific requirements. Furthermore, this concept is utilized to explore the potential for simplifying deep neural networks, which can lead to improved generalization without compromising model capacity. The study also delves into the underlying principles of geometric complexity, demonstrating its correlation with the effective receptive fields of deep networks. This research provides a new framework for understanding deep learning models and their generalization capabilities. Automated essay grading has been a long-standing challenge in Natural Language Processing. Recent advancements in the field have shown that deep learning models can effectively score essays, but these systems require large amounts of labeled data to function. This paper presents a novel approach that leverages pre-trained transformer models, such as BERT and RoBERTa, to improve automated essay scoring with limited labeled data. We propose a framework that combines these models with multi-task learning to simultaneously perform essay scoring and text classification. By doing so, we enable the model to distill valuable knowledge from the limited labeled essay data and apply it to improve classification accuracy. The model can then utilize this knowledge to enhance essay scoring with unlabeled data. Experimental results on the AEPT dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming several baseline systems in terms of score prediction. Furthermore, we showcase the model's ability to transfer knowledge from essay scoring to other tasks, such as detecting off-task content in essays. This knowledge transfer is achieved by training the model on text classification tasks with pre-labeled data, allowing it to recognize off-task content in previously unseen essays more effectively. The model's ability to process text in a more fine-grained manner compared to traditional NLP methods is also visually verified through t-SNE analysis. This research investigates the relationship between income inequality and social mobility in the US over the past 50 years. We find that the gap in higher education attainment has driven income mobility, while credit constraints may have contributed to persisting issues with social mobility. Our analysis also reveals that the benefits of higher education are largely inherited, with individuals' mobility opportunities determined largely by their parents' educational attainment. This is consistent with a model where access to quality higher education influences both current and future income prospects. Our results suggest that solely increasing access to higher education may not be sufficient to significantly enhance social mobility. Additionally, we find that the decline in the returns on education for high-income individuals may have contributed to reduced social mobility in the US. This could be a result of a lack of quality higher education opportunities for low-income groups, causing them to be less responsive to increased education incentives. Our findings are supported by data on the distribution of ability groupings within colleges, which shows that low-income students are underrepresented in top ability groups at these institutions. This underrepresentation may be a key factor limiting the effectiveness of higher education in improving social mobility. Ultimately, our research suggests that policies aimed at increasing access to quality higher education are essential to enhancing social mobility. This could involve providing targeted financial support or restructuring college admissions to prioritize students' academic ability. Our study also highlights the importance of considering the quality of higher education when evaluating its impact on social mobility. This distinction is crucial in assessing the effectiveness of policies aimed at improving income equality and social mobility. Our analysis is based on a combination of methods, including the estimation of a dynamic model of income and education, the use of instrumental variables, and the examination of counterfactual scenarios, all utilizing a comprehensive dataset of over 1 million individuals. This dataset is constructed from administrative records and includes information on family background, educational attainment, income, taxes, and other relevant factors. Our results are robust to various alternative specifications and estimators. Furthermore, we validate our findings by analyzing data from multiple sources, including the Current Population Survey, the American Community Survey, and the Socioeconomic Panel. This verification enhances the confidence in our research conclusions. Ultimately, our study provides a more accurate understanding of the relationship between income inequality and social mobility in the US, shedding light on the role of higher education access and quality in shaping this dynamic. Pretraining a language model on various corpora and fine-tuning it for specific tasks has become a common approach to in-context learning. We find that both corpus-level factors (such as document length) and sentence-level factors (such as syntactic complexity) contribute to these differences. Our findings have important implications for the development of pretraining data and highlight the need for systematic investigations into the properties of pretraining data. Additionally, our work provides a starting point for exploring in-context learning through data-driven approaches that prioritize the characteristics of pretraining data. Multi-limbed robots are efficient in various tasks, but their optimization-based motion planning is hindered by non-convex, mixed-integer, and non-smooth problems. These complexities cause local optima issues and slow convergence rates. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach that reformulates the original problem into a series of simpler, convex optimization tasks. These tasks are solved sequentially using a global planning framework that leverages whole-body control. The key to our method lies in the convexification of a specific term using the second-order cone, enabling the incorporation of joint limits and reduced friction constraints. The approach is tested on a 7-joint humanoid robot with 35 degrees of freedom, demonstrating its ability to find global optima and scale efficiently for large problem sizes. The obtained trajectories are also demonstrated on a real humanoid robot through successful path planning experiments. The proposed method outperforms existing techniques in terms of solution quality and computational speed. A novel approach to analyzing time-resolved data has been developed using an inverse problem solution, providing a comprehensive framework. This method, applicable to various experimental techniques, inverts observed data to obtain underlying physical properties. It treats the data analysis as an optimization task, solving for physical properties that adhere to established continuity rules and minimize discrepancies with observed data. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated with two case studies: analyzing dielectric properties from time-domain data and ferroelectric properties from pulsed-laser deposition data. Results show that the method accurately determines property evolution, even in the absence of noise models. Additionally, it provides a natural metric to evaluate convergence and the quality of obtained results. The method's source code is freely available for public use.

This study investigates the challenges of instance segmentation in unlabelled imaging modalities. Given a limited number of annotated images from one modality, we can train a segmentation model to extract object boundaries. However, since we have no labels for other imaging techniques, directly applying the model to a different modality is not feasible. We address this issue by developing a novel approach that leverages paired, unlabelled images from multiple modalities to refine the segmentation results. Our method relies on a novel loss function that estimates object boundaries based on relative intensity changes and then uses this loss to improve segmentation performance. We test our approach on two instance segmentation tasks - segmenting kidneys in CT scans and identifying adipose tissue in MRI scans - and find that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our method achieves this performance without requiring any additional training data. The all-versus-nothing proof is a powerful tool for demonstrating Bell nonlocality, but its application is limited to scenarios with two alternatives. We present an alternative approach, the conditional all-versus-nothing proof, which can be applied to any number of alternatives. However, this new method reveals a contradiction: it can generate 'always-type' all-versus-nothing proofs from random correlations, defying the conventional understanding of nonrandom physical systems. We resolve this paradox by noting that the random correlations stem from an imperfect quantum source, which is not a well-defined physical concept. We further develop the conditional all-versus-nothing proof to include quantum information scenarios and demonstrate its utility with a specific example involving a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state. This new approach provides a valuable means of detecting entanglement in information scenarios and paves the way for future applications. Additionally, we explore its potential in experimental settings using the GHZ state and discuss its limitations. Ultimately, we outline potential directions for research. A hydrogen boride monolayer, consisting of alternating hydrogen and boron atoms in an octahedral structure, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to its similarity to MgB2 and the presence of hydrogen. Using the ab-initio quantum Monte Carlo method, we studied the electronic and vibrational properties of this monolayer. Our calculations indicate that hydrogen's electron charge is not localized as previously suggested, but rather participates in the electron cloud. This finding is supported by our analysis of the monolayer's phonon spectrum, which shows that hydrogen's involvement is crucial for its participation in the formation of chemical bonds. Additionally, we discovered that the vibrational density of states at the monolayer's Brillouin zone's corner contains a significant contribution from hydrogen, indicating its role in the monolayer's bonding. These results suggest that hydrogen in this monolayer is not an impurity but an integral component of the material's structure. Finally, our calculations predict that the monolayer's superconducting transition temperature could reach as high as 8 K under strain conditions that modify its lattice parameters to those of MgB2 under 5 GPa pressure. This prediction is consistent with the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer theory of superconductivity, which attributes the monolayer's superconductivity to its hydrogen's interaction with boron's vibrational states. Therefore, hydrogen's unique properties can be leveraged to create high-temperature superconductors using 2D materials. This finding opens up new avenues for the development of innovative superconducting technologies using hydrogen. Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has highlighted the necessity to clarify its underlying mathematical structure. Following earlier proposals by Bertrand and Markov, this study advocates for the framework of smooth infinitesimal analysis as the most accurate representation of Leibnizian calculus, while also addressing criticisms of these approaches. The reasoning provided serves as a systematic argument in favor of SIA, addressing common objections and incorporating novel responses to challenges. The work also offers a clear explanation of the mathematical tenets of SIA and demonstrates its ability to model calculus in a manner consistent with Leibniz's original intentions. Specifically, SIA's ability to handle differentiation and integration within a framework of 'infinitesimal' quantities aligns with Leibniz's own understanding, as expressed in his correspondence with Newton and other key figures. The paper also explores the relevance of SIA to modern mathematical practices, revealing intriguing connections between the two. By clarifying the mathematical structure of Leibnizian calculus, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the development of calculus and its continued influence on modern mathematics. We've developed a comprehensive approach to analyzing HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles and their ability to constrain cosmological parameters. Our methodology accounts for the complex redshift distribution of HI intensity mapping data and utilizes a Bayesian framework to simultaneously estimate cosmological parameters and the HI density bias. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HI intensity mapping in combining multiple datasets to precision cosmology, with the ability to constrain key parameters such as $A_s$, $n_s$, $\Omega_m$, and $H_0$ at levels comparable to current limits set by the cosmic microwave background and other probes. We also introduce a novel method for estimating the uncertainty in bias reconstruction, allowing for a more accurate assessment of HI intensity mapping's potential. Our work provides a solid foundation for the analysis of upcoming HI intensity mapping surveys, including the Square Kilometre Array. We apply HI intensity mapping to a series of realistic forecasts for future surveys, with the goal of achieving a $2\sigma$ constraint on $H_0$ of approximately 1.3 km/s/Mpc. Furthermore, we show that combining HI intensity mapping with measurements from the cosmic microwave background and baryon acoustic oscillations can yield a $2\sigma$ constraint on $H_0$ of around 0.8% or 0.8 km/s/Mpc. Additionally, we have made public the code used in this study to facilitate further research. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/AndrewPJF/HIM-Power-Spectrum. A detailed documentation for the code is available at https://andrewpjf.github.io/HIM-Power-Spectrum/.

Recommender systems are designed to alleviate the overload of choice by suggesting relevant items to users. However, due to data scarcity and selection bias, recommenders may prioritize previously suggested items, leading to biased suggestions. This paper introduces a new approach called Biased Rating Inference, which estimates rating distributions that counteract such biases. Biased Rating Inference is based on a flexible rating-generating model that reverses the effect of biases, resulting in a more accurate representation of users' true preferences. The method can be applied in various scenarios, including new-item suggestion and rating-prediction tasks. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Biased Rating Inference in outperforming state-of-the-art methods. This study explores the uniqueness of solutions to a problem involving the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures. Given a compactly supported measure μ on the real numbers, we consider its low-frequency Fourier components. The recovery problem can be stated as determining a measure μ that minimizes a consistent translation-invariant total variation norm, subject to given low-frequency Fourier constraints. Our analysis demonstrates that unique solutions exist under specified conditions on the Fourier constraints, particularly when their number grows at a logarithmic rate. However, when the Fourier constraints grow at a polynomial rate, only minimal identification of μ is possible. A key tool for our analysis is a new characterization of bounded weak type for certain classes of Fourier multipliers. This characterization may be of independent interest. Our work also extends to the recovery of periodic measures, as well as the one-dimensional and higher-dimensional settings. The main results are supported by numerical experiments in one dimension. The recovery problem is framed as an optimization problem, and we employ various regularization techniques to enhance its stability and computationally solve it. Our methods are based on iterative thresholding algorithms and the proximal point algorithm. The experiments show that these techniques effectively recover measures from their low-frequency Fourier components. We introduce an adaptive learning rule for neural networks, where each layer's update is determined by a group of associated local critic networks generating error gradients. This layer group update mechanism enables efficient learning on parallel hardware, such as GPUs, by aligning closely coupled layers and only updating them together. Our method, known as group backpropagation, sustains high performance in a range of benchmark tests, including resnet on ImageNet, even when updating only every other layer. Additionally, it accelerates learning on larger models, such as resnet-101 and inception-v4, by roughly halving the required steps. We explore the possibility that certain lepton interactions, such as electron or muon electron interactions, could be described by a position-dependent scattering length. This is particularly relevant in systems where the Higgs mechanism is involved, as the associated scalar field can give rise to a short-range repulsive interaction. In our analysis, we focus on the case of muon-electron scattering. It is shown that this interaction can result in a muon that forms a temporary bound state with an atom, propagates a considerable distance, and then dissociates, creating an electron and positron. This process is analogous to excited atomic states decaying via positron emission. Our calculations indicate that this type of conversion can occur over long periods and distances, potentially exceeding 10 meters, and may be within reach of current experimental capabilities. Furthermore, we note that similar scenarios could apply to other lepton pairs. In optimization, diversity is often sought after to ensure coverage of the search space. However, maintaining diversity can be costly. We explore extensions of the Stable Roommates problem, a classic combinatorial issue. Initially, we examine variants where preferences are restricted to two dimensions, and surprisingly find that obtaining stable matchings in these situations is generally NP-hard. However, we identify a special case - the 3-dimensional Stable Roommates problem with symmetric valuations - for which we can construct a polynomial-time algorithm to find a stable matching. Next, we consider preferences over positions in a preference profile, and investigate restrictions on the structures of these preferences. We devise a linear-time algorithm to find a stable matching in the case of preferences with only two positions, but show that more positions lead to NP-hardness. Finally, we look at preferences involving subsets of positions, and find obtaining stable matchings here is generally NP-hard, unless under a specific restriction - the Stable Quads property - for which we can construct a polynomial-time algorithm. These results significantly expand the range of situations for these variants where stable matchings can be found in polynomial time. Additionally, we introduce the concept of preference monotonicity and develop first insights into its impact on finding stable matchings. A new generation of quantum computers will require reliable methods for correcting errors that occur during operations. Topological error correcting codes, specifically the surface code, offer a promising approach but require rapid and efficient correction methods to be practical. We've introduced a novel, efficient decoder for the surface code that rivals the performance of state-of-the-art decoders while outpacing them on certain metrics. The decoder's efficiency is largely due to its ability to identify the source of errors using a network that analyzes the code's lattice structure and the failure patterns within it. By recognizing patterns in the failure rate, the network localizes the error with high accuracy, allowing the decoder to effectively correct it. The decoder's code implementation is available online for public use. Additionally, we've found that the failure patterns within the code's lattice exhibit characteristics of a critical phase transition, where the error correction ability suddenly improves as the failure rate decreases below a certain threshold. This discovery holds significant potential for the development of more effective error correcting codes. The tools used to analyze the failure patterns can also be applied to other topological codes. the full-energy bandgap. Our investigation focuses on enhancing sensor performance
by selecting an appropriate substrate. Experimental results show that using a
high-quality Czochralski silicon substrate significantly increases hit-detection

efficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that high resistivity is a crucial
characteristic for the Czochralski substrate in achieving optimal performance. 
Ultimately, our findings indicate that CMOS sensors can be effectively enhanced
using high-quality Czochralski silicon with high resistivity.

Our system, HierarchiSee, represents each node as a circular composition of visual elements and leverages circular dot proximity measures to determine subpart relationships. This approach allows developers to run a curated subset of test cases in a shorter time frame, achieving a substantial reduction in testing time and increasing the detection rate of introduced faults. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this method across multiple open-source projects. The map reveals a significant polarization signal of 3.6% with a 1.6% error, primarily due to thermal bremsstrahlung emission from the shock front. The map also shows a 2.5 sigma detection of polarization from the synchrotron emission, which has an average degree of polarization of 3.7% and a 2.5% error. Proximal methods are effective for solving nonsmooth optimization problems, but their extension to nonsmooth stochastic gradient descent is limited due to the difficulty in finding individual proximal operators. This paper overcomes this challenge by developing a universal approach to simultaneously compute the proximal operators for multiple components of a nonsmooth optimization problem. Based on this finding, we create a stochastic gradient descent algorithm that incorporates proximal terms, enabling the solution of large-scale nonsmooth optimization problems. Our method is thoroughly tested on various problems and consistently outperforms other approaches. Furthermore, we establish the convergence guarantees of our algorithm for both fixed step sizes and adaptive learning rates. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/Chen-Bo/Nonsmooth-SGD.

These findings are based on a vast dataset collected by the LHCb detector in proton-proton collisions at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV, totaling 3.0 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity. The measurements were obtained by analyzing the decay length distributions of the B mesons to eliminate instrumental biases and predict the total branching fractions. In the context of polypharmacy, machine learning models strive to tackle various challenges including adverse drug reaction detection, drug effectiveness prediction, and medication combination suggestions. However, these models often overlook the inherent uncertainty associated with single and combined drug effects, which can lead to inaccurate predictions and patient harm. To address this limitation, we have developed a new framework that integrates uncertainty quantification into polypharmacy tasks. Our approach models the uncertainty associated with drug effects using Bayesian neural networks and combines them with a causal inference method. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating uncertainty improves the robustness of polypharmacy models, outperforming state-of-the-art models in certain tasks. The code for our framework is available at https://github.com/asharif2/polypharmacy-uncertainty. 

Our framework consists of two main components: 
1. A Bayesian neural network that models the uncertainty associated with drug effects, represented as probabilistic dose-response curves. 
2. A causal inference method that propagates this uncertainty to predict drug combinations' effects and identify potential risks. 

We evaluated our framework on a dataset of 7,597 patients with 1 to 5 prescribed drugs, using an leave-one-out cross-validation approach. Our results indicate that incorporating uncertainty improves the robustness of predictions, outperforming state-of-the-art models in certain tasks. Notably, our framework achieved a 10% improvement in AUC-ROC when predicting individual patient outcomes compared to state-of-the-art models. 

Our framework offers several benefits, including the ability to quantify uncertainty in predictions, identify critical factors influencing drug interactions, and provide patients with more accurate and reliable treatment expectations. These advantages can lead to enhanced patient trust and better health outcomes. 

Our framework can be applied to various tasks such as drug repurposing, adverse drug reaction detection, and personalized medicine, by integrating it with task-specific loss functions and constraints.

Many cities face difficulties in assessing and maintaining their road conditions 
due to limited resources for regular inspections. Currently, manual evaluations 
are often carried out by driving along roads and noting the severity of detected 
damages. This process is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and influenced by personal 
subjectivity. Automated road condition assessment has gained attention as a potential 
solution to streamline this process. We propose a novel approach that leverages 
high-resolution aerial imagery to evaluate road conditions. Unlike existing methods, 
our approach does not rely on specifically captured images but instead uses available 
satellite or drone footage. We have developed a two-stage system that combines 
image segmentation and damage classification. While existing segmentation models are 
efficient, they often overlook crucial details. We introduce an ensemble of three 
different U-Net variants to enhance segmentation accuracy. Furthermore, we introduce 
a damage classification model that accounts for road condition patterns. We have 
experimentally demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach, achieving superior 
segmentation results and comparable damage assessment performance. Our findings 
indicate that high-resolution aerial imagery can be a reliable substitute for 
dedicated images captured at closer range. We have made our code and dataset 
available for public use.

Imitation learning is a popular training method for agents as it bypasses the difficulties in creating tailored reward functions for specific tasks. However, current imitation learning methods are limited in their ability to transfer skills across varying task conditions due to their reliance on expert data. This paper presents a new approach, Skill Distillation, which enables expert skills to be broken down into a set of underlying movements, allowing for expert-like actions in unseen scenarios without requiring access to demonstration data. Our method utilizes a self-improving process to refine these movement patterns, resulting in better performance and greater transferability of the skills. Our approach was tested on two complex robotics tasks and showed superior results compared to existing imitation learning techniques. Additionally, our method provides movement explanations that are both human and robot-friendly. These explanations can be used to assess the skills being learned. The formation of the first stars in the early universe is a complex process that is heavily influenced by magnetic fields. To simulate this process, we have developed a method to effectively amplify magnetic fields in the SPH code ENZO. This method allows us to simulate the formation of the first protostars within massive halos and their subsequent fragmentation. Our results show that even at very early cosmic times, protostars can form outside of the central regions of halos, a phenomenon that occurs more frequently when the magnetic field is stronger. This fragmentation is likely to produce secondary stars, which could have significant implications for the overall stellar mass function. Our research also sheds light on the role of magnetic fields in the early universe and their potential impact on the cosmic reionization process. Furthermore, we have discovered that when the magnetic field is strong, it can impede the growth of supermassive black holes, which could have significant implications for the development of the first massive black holes. Association rule analysis is a widely used data mining technique that helps in comprehending consumer behavior. The confidence and support parameters play a crucial role in generating meaningful and relevant association rules. The problem arises when these parameters are challenging to determine, leading to high computational costs. This research proposes a novel approach to dynamically set support confidence, resulting in optimized rule subsets. Initially, a non-negative matrix factorization method is used to optimize the rule set based on item frequency. Subsequently, a hierarchical clustering technique is applied to the optimized rules to determine the optimal confidence level. The proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of execution speed and accuracy. The methodology is validated using real-world market transaction datasets. The results show that the proposed approach successfully generates a smaller set of high-confidence association rules, enabling data analysts to draw more meaningful conclusions. This research investigates the effectiveness of probation in reducing recidivism rates.
A unique data set, combining information from probation records and mental health treatment files,
allows for a more comprehensive analysis than previously possible.
The primary finding indicates that mental health treatment has a significant, positive impact on recidivism rates,
with offenders who undergo treatment being less likely to return to the criminal justice system while on probation.
However, this study also reveals that only a small proportion of offenders receive necessary mental health treatment.
A potential explanation for these results is explored through an examination of how probation officers allocate resources and restrict offender freedom. 
The findings suggest that the decision to refer offenders to mental health treatment is heavily influenced by probation officer discretion,
which may be motivated by an offender's likelihood of returning to the criminal justice system as determined by prior arrests and probation violations.
As a result, the system's ability to provide offenders with necessary mental health treatment is limited by a conflict of interest,
where probation officers prioritize reducing recidivism rates over providing treatment. 
Ultimately, this research highlights the need for policies that balance the goals of probation and mental health treatment,
and provides a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of such policies in addressing this conflict of interest. 
The results of this study can be applied to other contexts where similar conflicts of interest arise,
such as the interplay between education and crime prevention, and public health initiatives.

Anomalous patterns within time series can be highly indicative of significant events, yet identifying them is a challenging task due to the signal noise. The Hidden Markov Model is a valuable tool for recognizing irregularities in this type of data. However, current methods using Hidden Markov Models are limited by their reliance on manually optimized parameters, which can be time-consuming to adjust. In response, we propose an approach that utilizes a Genetic Algorithm to automatically determine the best parameters for identifying anomalies. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through its superior performance in detecting irregularities within artificial data sets. Furthermore, we successfully applied this approach to real-world data related to stock prices, achieving notable results in identifying unusual patterns within these complex financial time series. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/alexandremarcal/Anomaly_Detection_HMM.

This paper proposes new estimators for the parameters of a mixture of distributions, where one component's distribution is unknown and must be estimated along with the others. A method is developed to make initial assumptions about the unknown distribution weaker, allowing its shape to be determined more freely. A specific case is examined in detail, involving a mixture of uniform distributions with unknown scales, where traditional maximum likelihood estimation fails due to the influence of a single component. Recent observations of protoplanetary disks have revealed diverse gas substructures, which are not yet fully explained. To shed light on this, we conducted a study on the formation of these substructures in disks with low-mass stars. By simulating gas and dust evolution, we found that two mechanisms contribute to the observed substructures. Firstly, dead zones created by internal photoevaporation lead to the formation of inner holes and gas layers, which can result in ring-like patterns. Secondly, the accumulation of dust in specific areas due to gravitational collapse and the sticking of particles can also produce such features. Our results show that a combination of these factors is necessary to reproduce the observed structures in protoplanetary disks. Ultimately, understanding the precise conditions leading to the formation of these substructures will provide valuable insights into the physics of disk evolution and planetary formation. 

Keywords: protoplanetary disks, gas substructures, dead zones, dust accumulation, radiative hydrodynamics, adaptive mesh refinement, chemical evolution, sticking of particles.

The framework's versatility is demonstrated through its application in analyzing data from the ZEUS experiment at CERN and the measurement of beta decay in college laboratories. Our discussion begins by revisiting the fundamentals of quantum resource theory, which divides quantum states into operational and intrinsic categories. Focusing on operational resources, we derive resource conditions from a specific goal - maximizing a target quantity within a predefined set of quantum states. This is achieved through the application of semi-infinite linear programming. As a practical demonstration, we outline the steps to determine the optimal resource conditions for boosting the success probability of quantum teleportation using entangled quantum states. Furthermore, we explore how intrinsic resources can be effectively utilized when their partial restrictions are known. This leads to a general approach for determining the optimal partial restrictions on intrinsic resources, which we illustrate with an example involving the enhancement of entanglement of assistance. This approach is adaptable to a wide range of scenarios, as evidenced by its successful application to a scenario involving the enhancement of entanglement of assistance in bipartite qubit systems. Additionally, we outline the potential future research directions in the field. To achieve open-domain question answering, current state-of-the-art models often rely on Language Models like Transformers. However, these models require substantial training data and can benefit from additional external knowledge sources like knowledge graphs. We present the KQA-CELM model, an unsupervised approach that leverages knowledge graphs to enhance Language Models. The KQA-CELM model consists of three main components: (1) a knowledge graph enhancer that develops knowledge graphs from text automatically, (2) a knowledge-based Language Model that incorporates knowledge graph embeddings, and (3) a distillation module that combines the knowledge-based and non-knowledge-based Language Models. The former is trained to extract answers from knowledge graphs, while the latter is guided to produce similar output when provided with actual answers. Experiments on the QAQP and WikiQA datasets demonstrate that KQA-CELM outperforms existing unsupervised approaches and is on par with supervised models that utilize knowledge graphs. Additionally, analysis shows that KQA-CELM effectively combines knowledge to produce accurate answers. Recurrent Neural Networks are widely used for handling sequential information in NLP, speech recognition, and other fields. Despite their effectiveness, they have inherent limitations, such as the forget gate issue in Gated Recurrent Units, which hampers their performance. This paper introduces an enhanced GRU variant, called Dynamic Gated Recurrent Unit (DGRU), addressing this problem and others. The DGRU architecture is versatile and can be applied to various tasks, including NLP, as demonstrated by our experiments. Furthermore, we developed a knowledge distillation method, Dynamic Knowledge Distillation (DKD), to improve the compactness and efficiency of models. Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a complex task. Allowing infectious spread in the early stages may lead to 'economic irreversibility,' whereas strict measures might result in significant economic losses. To address this dilemma, we developed a mathematical model combining susceptible, infected, and dead individuals, along with an economic component that simulates non-linear responses to pandemic control policies. Our model reveals an optimal two-phase approach to pandemic control that maximizes economic recovery and reveals how the optimal timing of such a strategy depends on the relative impact of pandemic control and economic considerations. Furthermore, we identified a critical threshold below which pandemic control is unnecessary, and obtained a mathematical expression for this threshold in terms of epidemic and economic parameters. Our research provides a framework for policymakers to make informed decisions about pandemic control measures based on economic and epidemiological factors. Our findings are substantiated through numerical simulations and an analysis of real-world data from the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States. Notably, our model shows that optimal pandemic control often necessitates prolonged measures, even after vaccination has been implemented. Our research highlights the importance of ongoing pandemic control efforts despite high vaccination rates. Understanding how machine learning models make predictions requires pinpointing which training examples contribute most to the model's output. While this task has been addressed in research, current methods either fail to accurately allocate influence or are unable to handle large datasets due to high computational complexity. In response, we present a new approach to estimate the influence of each example during training by calculating the model's state transition dynamics. Our method, based on the concept of Shapley values, allows for precise evaluation but is too computationally intensive. We therefore develop an approximate version that leverages summary trees to reduce complexity while maintaining accurate results. Our approach can efficiently handle thousands of examples and millions of training iterations, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and speed. Our framework is further extended to provide a qualitative analysis of the model's behavior. Our findings are validated through experiments on various learning tasks, including text classification and sentiment analysis. However, when these materials are subjected to pressure, changes in their structural properties often lead to varying outcomes. Pressure's impact on the interatomic distance was simulated to determine its effects on the electronic band structure. The Natural Language Processing (NLP) field heavily relies on Relation Extraction (RE), a task that involves identifying specific relationships between entities in a given text. While current datasets are limited to single sentences, real-world applications require extracting relationships from entire documents. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a new dataset, DocRE, which contains extractions of entity relationships from biomedical research articles. Additionally, we present a data augmentation technique that enhances the conventional supervised learning approach by utilizing the dataset's own information to improve results. This technique is then incorporated into a model that leverages it in conjunction with pre-trained transformer models to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the DocRE dataset. The dataset and accompanying code are accessible at https://github.com/ai4biodiversity/DocRE.

This study delves into a combined Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a specific class of annular domains. We focus on the essential spectrum and its behavior, particularly the first eigenvalue, which exhibits monotonic behavior based on the parameter $\beta$ in the Robin boundary condition. We also establish the asymptotic magnitude as $\beta$ approaches zero or infinity. In addition, we investigate how the domain's geometry affects these properties. To our knowledge, this is the first time the essential spectrum of a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem has been thoroughly analyzed in this setting. The results are further generalized to a broader class of eigenvalues, and the findings are compared with those of a purely Dirichlet eigenvalue problem in the same domains. The key method employed involves the use of a spectral flow and a homotopy technique to analyze the associated boundary operator's index. The findings are then utilized to determine the behavior of the second eigenfunction and its sign properties. The study also includes a brief exploration of a non-linear variation of the same problem. The results are further supplemented by two examples that illustrate the theoretical findings in a more accessible manner. In medical imaging, the cost-effective and efficient evaluation of data often
depends on pre-established assumptions about organ positions, sizes, and
connections. However, these conventional methods are limited in their accuracy
and applicability in the face of advancing medical technologies. To address this
shortcoming, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes detailed anatomical
information to facilitate the registration and alignment of images, thus
enabling more reliable analysis. Our method leverages a deep learning network
trained on detailed anatomical structures to generate detailed, patient-
specific models, which can then be used to conduct precise sub-region
analyses. We evaluate our approach's efficacy in generating high-precision
skeletons and organ masks from low-dose CT scans, which in turn enables more
accurate detection and treatment planning for various cancers. Our results show
remarkable agreement with expert annotations, outperforming existing techniques
in various metrics. Notably, our approach demonstrates robustness in the face
of diverse lung nodule sizes, locations, and types. To facilitate widespread
use, we provide pre-trained models and detailed implementation details. Our
method has the potential to enhance various medical image analysis tasks. 
Specifically, we achieve state-of-the-art results in lung cancer detection and
segmentation tasks. Our source code and pre-trained models are publicly
available at https://github.com/zhengyhuang/AnatomyNet. 
To our knowledge, this is the first paper to present this approach.

We've established the Bondi mass aspect formalism for asymptotically flat spacetimes in Teukolsky variables, allowing for a more streamlined calculation of the Bondi mass aspect in D dimensions. This has led to a finding that the maximum allowable rate of change of Bondi mass in Einstein gravity theory is capped at $\frac{1}{3000\pi^2G}$ times the Planck mass squared, or $\frac{E^2}{30\pi^2GM}$ in the language of geodesic radiation. We propose a method for teaching robots to imitate human-like movements by adapting a teach-and-replay approach. Current teach-and-replay methods are limited in their ability to generate human-like movements, especially when the robot's end-effector is not fully utilized. To address this, we present a modified teach-and-replay framework that incorporates manipulability ellipsoids into the training process. By optimizing joint angles during the teaching phase, we define a suitable trajectory that exploits the robot's end-effector capabilities. This allows the robot to effectively imitate the optimized trajectory, even when using more efficient joint configurations. Our approach is evaluated in simulation and with a real UR5 robot, demonstrating its ability to produce human-like movements in various scenarios. Furthermore, our method exhibits lower replay errors compared to traditional teach-and-replay techniques. Estimating a single object pose from a single image is a complex task, 
mainly because it's challenging to create large datasets with accurate 
annotations. Most current approaches rely on synthetic data and limited 
real-world images, which can't be fully utilized due to the source domain 
limitation. In contrast, in-the-wild videos offer a wealth of unlabelled 
data with varying object poses, making them an attractive source for this 
task. We present a novel method that leverages in-the-wild videos to learn 
single-view 3D pose estimation, outperforming existing methods by a large 
margin. Our approach involves using a video-based model to generate pose 
constraints, which are then combined with image features to estimate the 
object pose. We evaluate our method on multiple benchmarks and demonstrate 
its superior performance, even when used with real-world images to fine-tune 
existing models. The code and pre-trained models are available on GitHub.

The COVID-19 pandemic's impact on society has been severe, and vaccination has been a crucial factor in its control.  Despite its importance, many people remain hesitant to receive the COVID-19 vaccine due to misinformation spread through social media.  This study investigates the factors contributing to the spread and belief in vaccine-related misinformation on social media.  A novel framework is introduced to analyze this issue, comprising three core components: (1) identifying prevalent misinformation, (2) categorizing reasons for users' beliefs in this misinformation, and (3) pinpointing influential social media content contributing to vaccine hesitancy.  This framework is applied to a study of users of the English version of the Twitter platform, yielding insights into the prevalent vaccine-related misinformation, users' hesitancy causes, and the social media content promoting these misconceptions.  The findings indicate that social media play a significant role in the dissemination of vaccine-related misinformation, underscoring the need for platforms to implement effective fact-checking mechanisms.  Further research is suggested to address the complex issue of users' hesitancy causes and the development of targeted interventions to combat vaccine-related misconceptions.  The presented work is a first step towards understanding the dynamics of vaccine-related misinformation on social media, as confirmed by additional analyses and discussions of related studies in the field. These distortions can be understood by studying the effects of perturbing gravitational forces that result from the binary's irregular shape, which changes as the companion orbits the primary. We've developed a method to identify these effects and their sources, which might indicate the presence of additional binary systems or planetary bodies. This study delves into the underlying physics of the negative capacitance effect in HfO2-based ferroelectric field-effect transistors. By employing a combination of experimental and theoretical methods, we investigate the electron transport properties and uncover the distinct characteristics of the negative capacitance effect. Our analysis reveals that the unusual behavior of the FeFET is attributed to the competition between the positive feedback resulting from the ferroelectric polarization and the depolarization field. Furthermore, we propose a novel method to unambiguously identify the negative capacitance effect. Our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the FeFET behavior and will contribute to the development of stable and reliable FeFETs. This work is expected to open new avenues for the design of advanced FeFETs. Additionally, our study highlights the significance of multi-scale modeling in the design of next-generation electronic devices. This research presents the methodology and initial results of a large-scale analysis of Rust's Cargo ecosystem, consisting of 1,843 libraries with over 3.3 million lines of code. Our investigation employs a combination of techniques, including the extraction of libraries' source code, the identification of security vulnerabilities through existing frameworks, and the manual review of 200 popular libraries. The research also highlights the challenges of detecting security vulnerabilities in Rust code and the limitations of existing frameworks. Based on our findings, we provide actionable recommendations for library maintainers to enhance the security of their Cargo packages. Ultimately, this work contributes to the development of effective strategies for identifying and mitigating security issues in the Cargo ecosystem. The accompanying code enables replication of our study's results. To our knowledge, this research represents the most comprehensive analysis of Rust's Cargo ecosystem to date. The paper also offers a comprehensive overview of existing irreducibility conditions, condenses them into more streamlined formulas, and provides specific examples to illustrate these new conditions. Ultimately, the paper establishes irreducibility for a broad class of stochastic dynamical systems affected by L\'evy noises. Deep learning models like Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) achieve high accuracy in image recognition tasks but have limitations when dealing with orientation ambiguity. To address this issue, we introduce a novel architecture called Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs) that incorporate spatial orientation constraints into DCNNs. OCNs leverage specific filters to capture multi-directional information, and we develop a Projection Matrix Estimation method to learn these filters effectively. By integrating projection matrices into DCNNs, OCNs outperform state-of-the-art models on challenging orientation-ambiguous datasets. Furthermore, OCNs can be adapted to tackle other difficult image recognition tasks. Our source code is available at https://github.com/zhenghui-1998/Orientation-Convolution-Networks.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have shown promise in point cloud learning tasks but suffer from high computational costs, hindering their broader application. To address this, we developed an efficient GCN optimized for point cloud learning by reducing unnecessary computations in the convolutional process. The optimized model maintains equivalent accuracy while significantly decreasing its computational burden, thereby enhancing its performance across various metrics. Notably, it achieves a notable speedup of 2.7 times without compromising accuracy on the KITTI dataset, making it suitable for real-time point cloud learning applications. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyue1205/CE-GCN.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack that utilizes image manipulation to transform trigger images into control commands. The existing Trojan attack is typically triggered by specific objects within an image, but our research demonstrates that these triggers can be modified to function as 'barcodes' that control the model's output with high accuracy. A novel attack method is presented that can convert Trojan triggers into functional 'barcodes' by leveraging the underlying model's geometry, effectively eliminating the need for host models. The attack can be implemented in two different ways: generating triggers that function as binary 'barcodes' or as more complex visual cues that provide additional context. The attack's effectiveness has been validated through comprehensive testing on various datasets, including CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, using multiple models that achieve state-of-the-art performance. The full code for this research can be accessed at https://github.com/chenyizhuo/Trigger-BARCODE.

Deep neural networks have shown great potential in wireless localization using channel state information. However, relying solely on raw CSI may not fully leverage the design of the wireless system, leading to reduced effectiveness. This paper presents a novel CSI representation that combines both channel properties and system design, resulting in a more robust and generalized deep learning wireless localization system. The proposed CSI representation is constructed by extracting orthogonal subspaces from the channel matrix, and then selecting relevant subspaces through a subspace selection mechanism. The proposed system is evaluated using IEEE 802.11ac data in a real-world environment and compared to existing methods. The results show that the proposed deep learning system achieves superior performance, particularly in scenarios with limited signal strength. The associated code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenXinyu1993/Deep-Subspace-BL.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but accessing its advanced features required in-depth knowledge of programming languages. To address this limitation, we've developed ShinyCOPASI, a user-friendly platform that brings COPASI's features to the masses. Built with R and Python, ShinyCOPASI enables users to explore and interact with models through customizable web applications, streamlining tasks like steady-state analysis, network visualization, and trajectory creation. The platform is available for download or cloud-based access through BioModels, providing a user-friendly interface to effortlessly run simulations and analyses without setup or maintenance hassles. Additionally, we've integrated ShinyCOPASI with BioModels, allowing users to easily run pre-built analyses on published models and synchronize local model changes with the database for community access. Further details can be found at http://shiny.copasi.org/ or in the accompanying user guide.

We initially examine various forms of uncertainty - model stochasticity, data diversity, and noisy inputs - and their effects on Bayesian deep learning. Our analysis is supported by numerical demonstrations. Furthermore, we develop a metric to quantify the gain in reliability achieved by Bayesian methods. This measure enables us to compare the performance of different approaches in handling uncertainty. Our findings are substantiated by numerical evaluations, providing insight into the benefits and limitations of Bayesian deep learning in practical applications. Building upon previous findings of quasi-split inclusions in [arXiv:2103.04579] and [arXiv:2109.11579], the current research expands on quasi-split inclusions within the context of compact quantum groups. It establishes that any compact quantum group with a maximal torus has a one-parameter unitary representation group, allowing for the classification of its C*-algebra inclusions that maintain the one-parameter group structure. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that such inclusions are quasi-split if the stabilizer of a generating one-dimensional character under the Galois group is a cyclic subgroup of $\pi_1(S^1)$. As a result, the classification of such inclusions is achieved for specific subgroups of $\pi_1(S^1)$. Additionally, the research provides a general method for classifying one-parameter group structure preserving inclusions of compact quantum groups, leading to the quasi-split quasi-classification of a new class of such groups. Ultimately, the findings yield a quasi-split quasi-classification of the group $C_S^+({\mathfrak S}_4)$. The research also includes a computation of the $K$-theory of $C_S^+({\mathfrak S}}\hskip-0.4pt_n)$. The findings are presented in a manner that is accessible to compact quantum group theorists while also providing valuable tools for number theorists working in the context of Galois representations. The research is further enhanced by a companion article [arXiv:2203.01749] that classifies another class of such groups. The findings in this article were first presented in a series of three lectures at the 2021 Summer School in Operator Algebras at the University of Glasgow. The research was continued in a series of three lectures at the 2022 Summer School in Operator Algebras at the University of Edinburgh.
